title: The Origins of R. G. Collingwood's Philosophy of History in his Philosophy of Religion, 1916–1943
abstract: Abstract This article argues that R.G. Collingwood's philosophy of history was deeply rooted in his early philosophy of religion as expounded in Religion and Philosophy (1916). Although scholars have tended to separate Collingwood's early religious ideas from his later writings, this study demonstrates that his theory of history was informed by his endeavour to solve the theological problems raised by what he regarded as the reductionism of two Oxford philosophical schools: realism and idealism. In response, he defended a conception of thought as a qualitatively distinct, irreducible activity, enabling him to reinterpret central Christian doctrines, such as the incarnation and atonement, in historical terms. Christ's omniscience, for example, was reconceived as the knowledge of a perfect historian who understood human motives without predetermining them. This dualist conception of thought prefigured the metaphysical premise of his later theory that history was the re‐enactment of past thoughts. The article traces how these themes, first articulated in theological contexts, informed his later works from Speculum Mentis (1924) to the Essay on Metaphysics (1940). It concludes that the origins of Collingwood's philosophy of history cannot be separated from his philosophy of religion: both emerged from a defence of human freedom, historical meaning, and Christian theism.
venue: The Heythrop Journal

title: The Third Link: Why a Triadic Essence Admits Exactly Two Processions
abstract: A long-standing objection to the triadic invariant's theological implications holds that the numerical coincidence between three factors (Pattern, Intent, Presence) and three divine Persons is derivationally inert — the Person-count comes from Aristotle's two-faculty psychology imported from outside, not from the factor structure itself. This paper closes the objection using two published results: the bisimulation proof of irreducibility (Shell, Wish, and Noise) and the structural filter eliminating every competing ontological ground via the Zero Test (The Self-Consuming Objection). The closure runs on the operational/ground asymmetry built into the factor definitions: Pattern and Intent are operational (they generate immanent acts when a simple essence reflects on itself), while Presence is the ground of actuality (it does not generate a procession — it IS the field in which processions occur). The warrant chain is made explicit: the physics program validates the definitions as structurally asymmetric; the definitions analytically entail the role-split; the split constrains the count. Divine simplicity is derived from the self-grounding requirement, not imported from classical theism. Two operational factors yield two processions; one ground factor yields one unoriginate source; 2 + 1 = 3 Persons.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Readability of Reality: From Knowability to Sign: A Metaphysical Inquiry into Meaning, Āyāt, and Their Grounds
abstract: Why can reality be known? The problem appears under many headings: the intelligibility of nature, the success of science, the applicability of mathematics, realism, representation, information, consciousness, and meaning. This monograph argues that these discussions intersect around a broader phenomenon that deserves explicit analysis. Reality is not merely orderly; it is repeatedly available for disciplined discovery. Human beings and other epistemic systems can encounter patterns, construct representations, expose them to correction, predict novel results, and accumulate knowledge across persons and generations. The study calls this phenomenon readability. Readability is defined as the objective availability of reality to constrained, corrigible, and progressively integrative inquiry. The concept is distinguished from order, intelligibility, information, meaning, and signification. Naturalism, physicalism, structural realism, informational and mathematical ontologies, and classical theism are compared without assuming that scientific success deductively proves any one of them. The final movement studies the Qurʾānic concept of āyāt as a framework in which revelation, nature, history, and the human self can function as domains of indication. The conclusion is deliberately qualified: the Qurʾānic theistic framework possesses distinctive resources for unifying objective order, the possibility of knowers, epistemic normativity, and signification, though the inference remains open to philosophical criticism.

title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle
abstract: This paper develops the Baysüngür Philosophical Views (BFG), a metaphysical framework concerning the relationship between divine foreknowledge, temporal human agency, and free will. The framework addresses the apparent tension between the claim that God possesses infallible and timeless knowledge of future events and the claim that human beings nevertheless make genuinely free choices. BFG distinguishes divine knowledge from causal coercion and argues that divine foreknowledge does not, by itself, constitute a causal explanation of human choice. Its central conceptual contribution is the Experience–Choice Cycle, represented as Ht → Dt → St → Ht+1, in which accumulated experience influences deliberation, deliberation leads to choice, and each choice contributes to the agent's subsequent experiential history. The framework further distinguishes decision-space possibility from counterfactual metaphysical possibility and examines the relationship between divine knowledge, causation, temporal ontology, alternative possibilities, and moral responsibility. BFG is compared with Boethian timelessness, classical theism, Islamic philosophical accounts of divine knowledge, compatibilism, incompatibilism, Frankfurt-style theories of responsibility, Molinism, and contemporary theories of time. The paper does not claim to provide a conclusively demonstrated solution to the problem of divine foreknowledge and free will. Rather, it presents BFG as a proposed metaphysical research program whose explanatory adequacy remains open to further analysis.

title: Conceptions of God and Epistemic Mediation: A Five-Layer Model Abstract Religious epistemology often moves too quickly from an explanation of how a conception of God is formed to conclusions about whether the resulting belief is justified or true. This article defends the thesis that these questions must be separated into five layers: formation, conception, propositional attitude, justification, and truth/reference. abstract: This preprint develops a five-layer epistemic model for analysing human conceptions of God. Its central claim is that five distinct questions must not be conflated: how a conception is formed, what that conception represents, which propositional attitude is adopted toward it, whether that attitude is epistemically justified, and whether the relevant proposition is true and successfully refers to its intended object. The framework is metaphysically conditional, although it is applied here within theistic realism to a transcendent God who exists independently of human minds and is conscious in an analogical rather than univocal sense. The paper distinguishes a minimally conscious transcendent reality from stronger hypotheses concerning a creative or explanatory relation to the universe, purposive relations with human beings, revelation, and communicative trustworthiness. Reasoning, experience, testimony, and revelation are not assigned a fixed epistemic hierarchy. Their evidential weight instead depends on reliability, conditional independence, alternative explanations, shared sources of error, counterevidence, and resilience to defeaters. The model also distinguishes propositional from doxastic justification, personal from public justification, and faith from propositional belief. It permits suspension of judgment where the available evidence is insufficient or balanced. The contribution is not a conclusive proof of theism, but an integrated and revisable framework for determining where psychological explanations, representational limitations, evidential considerations, and truth claims bear on religious belief without allowing any single level to determine the others automatically.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: God as a Unified Categorical Ground: Microphysical Fundamentality, Consciousness, and Panpsychism
abstract: Abstract Contemporary fundamental physics and classical theistic metaphysics appear to exert opposing pressures on our conception of ultimate reality. Microphysical fundamentalism holds that the structure of the physical world is grounded in microphysical entities and their properties, whereas classical theism is committed to a single, unified ultimate ground that is explanatorily prior to all finite reality. Although not formally inconsistent, these commitments generate a substantive metaphysical tension once questions of categorical underwriting are made explicit. Existing theologically sympathetic responses address this tension only at a cost: micropsychist panpsychism preserves microphysical fundamentality but fragments ultimate grounding in a way that sits uneasily with monotheism, while cosmopsychism secures metaphysical unity at the expense of the bottom-up motivations of microphysical fundamentalism. This paper develops a third option, Unified Categorical Basis Panpsychism (UCBP), which preserves the fundamentality of microphysical entities with respect to physical structure and composition while locating ultimate unity at the level of categorical grounding. The view openly posits a novel primitive: a single, irreducibly mental, internally differentiated categorical basis—identified with God—in virtue of which physical properties have the dispositional profiles they have and conscious experience is metaphysically possible. The paper argues that this posit is theoretically motivated, internally coherent, and explanatorily principled, and that UCBP thereby avoids both the combination problem facing micropsychism and the decomposition problem facing cosmopsychism.
venue: Sophia

title: Miracle Money and Contemporary Nigerian Pentecostalism: A Philosophical Analysis of Matthew 17:24-27
abstract: The contemporary doctrine of miracle money has become a notable feature of some Nigerian Pentecostalism, with Matthew 17:24-27 frequently invoked to justify expectations of supernatural financial provision. Despite its growing influence, the doctrine has received limited philosophical scrutiny, particularly regarding its epistemological justification and hermeneutical legitimacy. This study examines the relationship between the Matthean narrative of the coin in the fish's mouth and the contemporary doctrine of miracle money from the perspective of the philosophy of religion. Employing a qualitative methodology that integrates philosophical analysis with contextual biblical hermeneutics, the study critically evaluates the epistemic basis of miracle claims, the interpretive movement from biblical narrative to doctrine, and the ethical implications of contemporary Pentecostal teaching. The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision. It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant. The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief. The paper contributes to ongoing debates in the philosophy of religion by clarifying the relationship between biblical interpretation, miracle claims, and contemporary Pentecostal doctrine.
venue: IRASS Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences

title: Is God’s worship-worthiness vague?
abstract: Abstract Yujin Nagasawa has argued that treating absolute perfection as a necessary condition of worship-worthiness generates a vagueness problem. If worship-worthiness requires omniscience, omnipotence, and omnibenevolence, then it appears to hinge on God’s knowledge of a single proposition p : without knowledge of p , God would not be omniscient and therefore not worship-worthy. Yet such a small difference seems too trivial to ground the evaluative difference between worship-worthy and not worship-worthy. I argue that this problem arises only if absolute perfection is the single minimally sufficient threshold of greatness for worship-worthiness. I develop instead a gradable, dual-threshold account. On this account, a sufficient inequality in value establishes the lower threshold for worship-worthiness, while absolute perfection marks the intrinsic maximum of worship-worthiness. Distinguishing mere worship-worthiness from supreme or maximal worship-worthiness separates vagueness at the lower threshold from God’s status as supremely worship-worthy. I then defend the account against objections concerning the relational character and possible range of worship-worthiness. Finally, I argue that the account creates a difficulty for Nagasawa’s maximal God approach to perfect-being theism. If supreme worship-worthiness is understood normatively, then a being that falls short of absolute perfection may be worship-worthy without being supremely worship-worthy. Nagasawa’s approach therefore risks implying either that God is not supremely worship-worthy or that whichever being happens to be greatest in the available modal space is supremely worship-worthy.
venue: Religious Studies

title: From Experience to Ground: The Necessity of a Non Coercive Relational Basis
abstract: A transcendental derivation from the structure of determinate being establishes the agápēic ground with formal necessity — but it can only be approached from one direction. A reader who declines the founding premise has not yet been reached. This paper closes that gap by reversing direction entirely. Beginning not from the metaphysics of determination but from the structural features of finite experience — relationality, intelligibility, and agency — it asks what any adequate metaphysics must preserve as real and shows that a purely groundless relational ontology cannot meet those requirements. Without a non-derivative ground, intelligibility is brute and contingent; without a non-coercive ground, originating agency collapses into conditioned transmission; without a necessary ground, explanatory deferral is indefinite. The argument concludes that finite experience, taken seriously as a source of metaphysical constraint, requires a ground that is necessary, self-existent, intrinsically intelligible, relational, and non-coercive — the same structural characterisation the ARM series reaches by transcendental elimination from the other direction. The philosophical significance is architectural: the ARM ground cannot be declined from the metaphysical direction without denying that anything determinate exists, and it cannot be declined from the phenomenological direction without eliminating the very practices — reasoning, inquiry, explanation — by which the denial would have to be articulated. Ten objections are considered and replied to, including the anthropocentrism objection, the coherence of non-coercive necessity, and the identification with classical theism. This paper establishes Route 2 of the four genuinely independent convergent arguments assembled in the series meta-argument.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A Critical Analysis of the Cosmological Arguments
abstract: This paper critically examines how far cosmological arguments actually establish the existence and nature of God. Rather than treating the cosmological argument as a single proof, it distinguishes several major families of arguments, including the Kalām Cosmological Argument, Aquinas’s Five Ways, Leibnizian and contemporary arguments from contingency, and arguments from hierarchical dependence and grounding. The central question throughout is not merely whether these arguments point toward some ultimate explanation, but what exactly follows from each stage of the reasoning. Particular attention is therefore given to the transitions from a first cause to a necessary ground, from a necessary ground to Pure Act, and from Pure Act to the further attributes associated with classical theism, such as intellect, omniscience, will, free creation, uniqueness, omnipotence, and moral perfection. The paper also develops an abductive defense of explanatory rationalism. It argues that contingent reality gives us genuine explanatory contrasts and that there are reasons to continue seeking explanations rather than terminating in brute contingency. However, this is defended as a defeasible inference to the best explanation rather than as a deductive Principle of Sufficient Reason. Rationalist infinitism is treated as a stronger rival than brute contingency because it preserves explanation without requiring a final foundation. The conclusion is a position described here as Minimalist Agnostic Deism: a provisional commitment to a necessary ultimate ground of contingent reality, combined with agnosticism about its further nature. The paper argues that cosmological reasoning provides stronger support for necessary grounding than for the full classical conception of God, while leaving open the possibility that further philosophical arguments could justify additional attributes.

title: A person in the face of infinity and the second side of the "main question of philosophy" (historical-philosophical and general theoretical aspects)
abstract: Has the "main question of philosophy" become outdated? If it has, then the discussion between theistic religion and atheism has also become outdated. However, it is not only still relevant but is also unfolding with renewed vigor in the modern, post-secular stage of contemporary Russian society. This article attempts to examine the other side of the "main question of philosophy" – the knowability of the world from the perspectives of the worldview companions of materialism and idealism, which include atheism, evolutionism, scientism, and voluntarism on one side, and theism, creationism, anti-scientism, and providentialism on the other side, forming two opposing and polemic worldview poles, two possibilities of free human choice, and two systems of the most general "navigation" of human life. The research methods involve determining the volumetric relationships between concepts, logical operations of defining content and dividing the volume of a concept, thought experiments, inductive generalization, conditional-categorical reasoning in the denying mode, cross-cultural analysis, and analogical reasoning. From the standpoint of materialism and its worldview companions, the world is, in principle, knowable, since humans occupy the highest position in the hierarchical ladder of being, whereas in idealism, they do not occupy such a position, which means that materialism is associated with epistemological optimism, and idealism with epistemological pessimism. However, materialism does not deny the infinity of knowledge about the material world, and one of the author's conclusions, representing the novelty of this work, is the assertion that the doctrine of absolute and relative truth is possibly a masked acknowledgment of the knowledge process as an eternal pursuit of a receding horizon, as a result of which epistemological optimism turns into epistemological pessimism. In the idealistic-theistic understanding, infinity is conceived as rational and personal, which answers a person's questioning and cognitive efforts and opens itself to them, something that cannot be the case with infinity understood materially and atheistically, as it is irrational, impersonal, and indifferent to humanity with its hopes and aspirations. Thus, the epistemological, seemingly, pessimism of idealism, surprisingly, turns into epistemological optimism.
venue: Философская мысль

title: The Inversion of Greatness
abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being—a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible—this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Rather than assuming modal logic to get the argument off the ground, the book builds that ground first: it derives the claim that whatever is possible is necessarily possible, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility, rather than taking it as a starting axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change requires temporality, spatiality, and physicality, borne by time, space, and substance, and that these three are necessarily instantiated. That structure is what the book calls Nature. From there it argues that no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. The result blocks grounds specified as occupants of that domain, a divine intellect among them, while leaving essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals standing as burdened rather than refuted. The greatness classical theism reserved for God—eternity, self-existence, being the source of all possibility—is relocated to Nature itself, and no determinate, active ground is left able to stand wholly outside Nature while retaining the classical attributes. The argument is then extended outward: to a convergence with contemporary physics in which the cosmological singularity marks a boundary of description rather than a boundary of being; to an account of consciousness as Nature registering itself from within; and to a political theory in which freedom is maximum shared possibility, secured by degree on a floor of material and civic conditions. Along the way the book argues that Reality is nothing over and above Nature. A closing section applies the completed argument to classical theological doctrines, including a new treatment of the problem of evil.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Role of Private Evidence in Avoiding Epistemic Suspension of Judgment (Agnosticism) Regarding the Existence of God
abstract: According to the evidentialist approach, one’s final position on a proposition emerges from the balance between supporting and opposing evidence, and justifying that proposition requires considering (or weighing) all available evidence. Unlike theists and atheists—who interpret evidence to favor their own beliefs — the agnostic regards the evidence as neutral, whether due to ambiguity about what counts as evidence, the failure of individual items to establish the claim, or the equal weight of opposing evidence. In this context, “evidence” typically refers to public evidence accessible to all. Occasionally, however, private and non-shareable evidence may arise in favor of one side. The key question is whether such private evidence can challenge or outweigh public evidence and thereby lift the suspension of judgment. Based on this study’s findings, private evidence can be valid and effective in epistemic dilemmas that incline toward agnosticism, provided two conditions are met: it possesses independent epistemic grounding (evidence supporting evidence), and the opposing public evidence is not so overwhelmingly strong as to create a perfect symmetry. Keywords: Private Evidence; Agnosticism; Suspension of Epistemic Judgment; Theism; Atheism; Religious Experience. IntroductionThe dominant approach in religious epistemology holds that evidence ultimately determines the outcome of debates, with justification resting on the evidence one possesses while rejecting contrary evidence. Theists and atheists both claim that evidence conclusively supports their own stance. In contrast, the epistemic agnostic suspends judgment—often because of uncertainty about what qualifies as evidence, flaws in individual evidential items, or balanced weights among conflicting evidence. Although “evidence” normally denotes public, widely accessible proof, certain private evidence may persuade only a single individual or a limited circle of epistemic agents. This study explores whether and how private evidence can break the stalemate caused by evenly balanced public evidence.While agnosticism has been addressed in recent epistemological debates in the West and has seen limited discussion in Iran, the role of private evidence has not received systematic attention as a central focus. By examining the assumptions underlying agnosticism, the present research clarifies how private evidence may help one escape epistemic skepticism about God’s existence. It analyzes the types of evidence and their roles in two contexts—epistemic disagreement and suspension of judgment—and then establishes the conditions under which private evidence attains validity when it conflicts with public evidence. Materials and MethodsThe current study employs an analytical research methodology, examining arguments for the epistemic validity of private evidence both under ordinary conditions and in cases of conflict with public evidence. Research FindingsThe findings of the study show that four possibilities arise regarding the epistemic warrant of private evidence:Valid in ordinary circumstances but invalid in conflict.Valid in both ordinary and conflict situations.Invalid in both ordinary and conflict scenarios.Invalid in ordinary circumstances but valid when in conflict.These scenarios are theoretically conceivable, though not all have clear proponents among religious epistemologists. Various proposals have been made to address these possibilities. On the one hand, agnosticism produces no decisive conclusion and leaves us in epistemic indecision, which we ought to escape. On the other hand, privatizing epistemic structures and processes —grounding belief on factors beyond public scrutiny—undermines the accuracy of our epistemic representations. A balanced approach must reconcile these concerns. This study demonstrates that private evidence can resolve the problem of epistemic suspension if it meets two conditions:It enjoys its own independent epistemic support, ensuring it is not merely subjective.Competing public evidence is not so compelling as to undermine confidence in one’s private deliverances. Discussion of Results and ConclusionsConsidering the results of the present study, private evidence consists of data or testimony that is not publicly accessible and derives from an individual’s personal epistemic faculties. Its legitimacy is contested both under normal conditions and when it clashes with public evidence. Ordinarily, private testimony may be deemed valid if it can be reconciled with established public epistemic channels, for example, interpreting religious experience as a form of sensory or emotional perception. When public evidence for and against God’s existence is evenly balanced, the debate can slide into suspension of judgment—an agnostic impasse that is epistemically unsatisfactory. Introducing private evidence reshapes this impasse: evidence can no longer be regarded as wholly neutral, and the agent becomes fully justified in acting based on their private conviction. This position is defensible. Beyond the general warrant for private evidence like religious experience, such evidence is especially valuable in an epistemic stalemate.Individuals may legitimately rely on private evidence when two conditions hold: it has its own epistemic grounding, and the opposing public evidence is not overwhelmingly strong. In the specific case of belief in God, objections to theism are not so decisive as to weaken both public and private supports for belief. Moreover, the imperative to avoid unbelief—and its attendant epistemic shortcomings—further underscores the prudence of crediting private evidence when public and private testimonies diverge.

title: The Structure of Yearning: Bouzid's Rule (B+F=Nf) as an Axiological Framework for Virtue and Vice
abstract: Contemporary debates in the axiology of theism evaluate spiritual yearning based on its object (theistic, ultimate, or secular) or its quantity (moderate vs. excessive). However, this quantitative-objective approach fails to resolve core paradoxes, as it treats yearning as a continuous variable, ignoring its internal architecture and relation to consciousness. This paper addresses three methodological paradoxes: (1) The Axiological Paradox (Rubio, 2026): If Aristotelian virtue is a mean, and God's value is infinite, is yearning for God a necessary vice of excess? (2) The Structural Paradox (Anderson, 2026): Can gratitude stifle the yearning for redemption by creating an illusion of contentment with unredeemed suffering? (3) The Objective Paradox (Burkhart, 2026): Can yearning for sacred land be evaluated by the same metrics as yearning for a personal God? The central thesis: the solution lies not in measuring how much or toward what we yearn, but in understanding the architecture of yearning. This paper introduces a novel phenomenological framework: Bouzid's Rule of Conscious Existence (B+F=Nf). This model structurally distinguishes between Spontaneous Yearning (biological, suppresses the witness, ends in satiation) and Sovereign Yearning (conscious, where the witness exercises Veto Power over biological drives, generating existential meaning). Consequently, virtue or vice is determined by its architecture (is yearning sovereign [F] or co-opted [B]?) and the worthiness of the object (defined by absoluteness, limitlessness, and transcendence). Applying this framework to Islamic Sufism as a non-dominant worldview, the paper demonstrates that Sufi yearning (Shawq) particularly in the models of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, al-Ghazali, and Ibn Arabi is not an Aristotelian vice of excess, but the pinnacle of Sovereign Yearning, transcending the biological self (B) toward the Absolute (Nf). Furthermore, the paper integrates findings from network neuroscience on general intelligence (Wilcox et al, 2026) not as empirical proof, but as a structural parallel, mapping weak, long-range connections and modal control regions to the neural correlates of sovereign yearning and its veto power. Finally, it develops a Functional Ontological Proof: the Witness (F) performs five irreducible functions (witnessing, observing, discerning, consciousness, and writing), each requiring a transcendent object. For example, witnessing requires a Witness who does not forget; writing requires a Reader who never forgets. Since (B) is finite, the structure of sovereign yearning ontologically necessitates a transcendent Absolute (Nf), lest (F) be an evolutionary and cognitive absurdity. The missing link objection is addressed by distinguishing open yearning (potentially illusory) from transcendent yearning (which exceeds all possible objects in B). This proof rests not on a statistical gap, but on a category mistake (Ryle, 1949): measuring meaning (Nf) with the tools of structure (B) is a fundamental error.

title: The Structure of Yearning: Bouzid's Rule (B+F=Nf) as an Axiological Framework for Virtue and Vice
abstract: Contemporary debates in the axiology of theism evaluate spiritual yearning based on its object (theistic, ultimate, or secular) or its quantity (moderate vs. excessive). However, this quantitative-objective approach fails to resolve core paradoxes, as it treats yearning as a continuous variable, ignoring its internal architecture and relation to consciousness. This paper addresses three methodological paradoxes: (1) The Axiological Paradox (Rubio, 2026): If Aristotelian virtue is a mean, and God's value is infinite, is yearning for God a necessary vice of excess? (2) The Structural Paradox (Anderson, 2026): Can gratitude stifle the yearning for redemption by creating an illusion of contentment with unredeemed suffering? (3) The Objective Paradox (Burkhart, 2026): Can yearning for sacred land be evaluated by the same metrics as yearning for a personal God? The central thesis: the solution lies not in measuring how much or toward what we yearn, but in understanding the architecture of yearning. This paper introduces a novel phenomenological framework: Bouzid's Rule of Conscious Existence (B+F=Nf). This model structurally distinguishes between Spontaneous Yearning (biological, suppresses the witness, ends in satiation) and Sovereign Yearning (conscious, where the witness exercises Veto Power over biological drives, generating existential meaning). Consequently, virtue or vice is determined by its architecture (is yearning sovereign [F] or co-opted [B]?) and the worthiness of the object (defined by absoluteness, limitlessness, and transcendence). Applying this framework to Islamic Sufism as a non-dominant worldview, the paper demonstrates that Sufi yearning (Shawq) particularly in the models of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, al-Ghazali, and Ibn Arabi is not an Aristotelian vice of excess, but the pinnacle of Sovereign Yearning, transcending the biological self (B) toward the Absolute (Nf). Furthermore, the paper integrates findings from network neuroscience on general intelligence (Wilcox et al, 2026) not as empirical proof, but as a structural parallel, mapping weak, long-range connections and modal control regions to the neural correlates of sovereign yearning and its veto power. Finally, it develops a Functional Ontological Proof: the Witness (F) performs five irreducible functions (witnessing, observing, discerning, consciousness, and writing), each requiring a transcendent object. For example, witnessing requires a Witness who does not forget; writing requires a Reader who never forgets. Since (B) is finite, the structure of sovereign yearning ontologically necessitates a transcendent Absolute (Nf), lest (F) be an evolutionary and cognitive absurdity. The missing link objection is addressed by distinguishing open yearning (potentially illusory) from transcendent yearning (which exceeds all possible objects in B). This proof rests not on a statistical gap, but on a category mistake (Ryle, 1949): measuring meaning (Nf) with the tools of structure (B) is a fundamental error.

title: ТЕИЗМ В КОНТЕКСТЕ СОВРЕМЕННЫХ ФИЛОСОФСКИХ ДЕБАТОВ: КЕНОТИЧЕСКОЕ ИСТОЛКОВАНИЕ НАТУРАЛИСТИЧЕСКИХ ИДЕЙ
abstract: Статья посвящена исследованию возможности кенотической интерпретации одного из направлений современной натуралистической философии, а именно: меметической натуралистической теории, развиваемой в трудах Д. Деннета, Р. Докинза и С. Блэкмор. В статье демонстрируется всеохватывающий (претендующий на полное описание реальности) пафос натурализма, базирующийся на антитеистических и антисубъектных философских основаниях. Автор применяет к анализу философских предпосылок указанного течения, с одной стороны, установку американского философа-теиста Алвина Плантинги о тройственном характере современной философской ситуации, а с другой стороны, установку итальянского философа-постмодерниста Джанни Ваттимо о кенотическом импульсе, лежащем в основании истории западной философии как таковой. В заключение автор статьи приходит к выводу о том, что вопреки убеждению Алвина Плантинги натурализм не представляет по самой своей природе одного из «злейших врагов» теизма. Рассмотренный кенотически (на основании кенотической методологии) натурализм открывает перспективу теологии самоограничения (кенозиса) Бога в процессе творения мира, развитие которого не предопределено, то есть в некотором смысле самостоятельно, и включает развитие как физических, так и ментальных событий. Разумеется, указанная интерпретация возможна только на основании критического переосмысления философских оснований натурализма. Однако религиозно-философская и собственно теологическая новизна кенотического подхода к исследованию современных, на первый взгляд антитеистических философских тенденций заключается в разработке и признании разнообразных форм теологического дискурса «вне» и «по ту сторону» классического метафизического повествования. The article is dedicated to the study of the possibility of a kenotic interpretation of one strand of contemporary naturalistic philosophy, namely the memetic naturalistic theory developed in the works of D. Dennett, R. Dawkins, and S. Blackmore. The article demonstrates the all-encompassing (claiming to offer a complete description of reality) pathos of naturalism, which is grounded in anti-theistic and anti-subject philosophical premises. The author applies, in the analysis of the philosophical presuppositions of this current, on the one hand the position of the American theist philosopher Alvin Plantinga regarding the threefold character of the contemporary philosophical situation, and on the other hand the position of the Italian postmodern philosopher Gianni Vattimo concerning the kenotic impulse that lies at the foundation of the history of Western philosophy as such. In conclusion, the author comes to the view that, contrary to Alvin Plantinga’s conviction, naturalism does not, by its very nature, constitute one of the “most implacable enemies” of theism. Considered kenotically (on the basis of kenotic methodology), naturalism opens the prospect of a theology of divine self-limitation (kenosis) in the process of the world’s creation, the development of which is not predetermined — that is, in a certain sense autonomous — and encompasses the unfolding of both physical and mental events. Of course, this interpretation is possible only on the basis of critical rethinking of the philosophical foundations of naturalism. However, the religious-philosophical and specifically theological novelty of the kenotic approach to the study of contemporary, at first glance anti-theistic philosophical tendencies consists in elaborating and recognizing diverse forms of theological discourse “outside” and “beyond” the classical metaphysical narrative.
venue: The Quarterly Journal of St Philaret s Institute

title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 1
abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume I: Social Critique, Woke Capitalism, and the Sexual Wing of the Purity Economy develops a systemic critique of a contemporary moral-commercial order in which virtue, guilt, innocence, legitimacy, and symbolic absolution increasingly become institutionalized, administered, displayed, and commodified. The concept of the Moral Purity Industry (TMPI) designates a social field in which moral categories cease to operate solely as standards of conduct and become socially exchangeable resources: guilt is produced and managed, innocence must be publicly demonstrated and periodically renewed, legitimacy is symbolically conferred, and moral standing is mediated through institutions, markets, bureaucracies, platforms, therapeutic vocabularies, and reputational systems. The volume argues that this formation cannot adequately be reduced either to progressive ideology or to capitalism considered in isolation. It instead examines their convergence within a hybrid moral-commercial regime, in which progressive, therapeutic, feminist, and humanitarian vocabularies interact with corporate incentives, managerial structures, consumer markets, political signaling, and institutional administration. In this sense, the term “woke capitalism” is employed analytically rather than as a partisan political label: it identifies a structural conjunction between moral symbolism and economic organization rather than a specifically conservative or left-wing object of critique. The study therefore rejects both political reductionism and purely economic accounts of the phenomenon. Volume I proceeds in three stages. Part I, “The Moral Purity Industry as Social Order,” develops the conceptual architecture of TMPI through the production and circulation of guilt, provisional absolution, purity as social currency, moral spectacle, new forms of moral expertise, and the structural tendency toward continuously expanding standards of implication and purification. Part II, “Woke Capitalism and the Industrialization of Virtue,” examines corporate virtue, ESG and DEI structures, reputational insurance, compliance regimes, the market for symbolic absolution, the commodification of rebellion, digital amplification, and woke capitalism as a hybrid regime. Part III, “The Sexual Wing of the Purity Economy,” extends this analysis into contemporary sexual culture, examining the relationship between the Moral Purity Industry and the Consumerist Sexual Economy, including polyamory, ethical non-monogamy, therapeutic mediation, anti-monogamous discourse, and the construction of the “evolved” sexual subject as a form of moral distinction. Methodologically, the work combines social and socio-economic critique with genealogy and the author's broader integrative theoretical architecture. Genealogy is used diagnostically rather than as a claim of simple historical continuity. The analysis distinguishes documentary transmission from structural and archetypal recurrence and employs the Inversion–Metastasis–Sublimation (IMS) model, the Dharma–Theism–Secularism (DTS) axis, Cognitive Gynocentric Telegony (CGT), ideo-telegony, and symbolic imprinting to examine how older grammars of purification, contamination, mediated legitimacy, guilt, and absolution may survive through mutation and secularization. Historical materials are therefore not treated as antiquarian objects or as proofs of direct descent, but as instruments for illuminating recurring structural correspondences within the contemporary order. The central thesis of the volume is that contemporary moral life is increasingly organized through the interaction of symbolism, institutional administration, reputation, consumption, and economic incentive. What presents itself as moral progress may therefore also generate durable systems of mediation in which purity becomes performative, guilt renewable, legitimacy conditional, and absolution provisional. The Moral Purity Industry seeks to make this configuration analytically visible by treating morality and commerce not as separate domains but as mutually reinforcing components of a wider civilizational formation.

title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 2
abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume II: The Genealogy of Purification: From Manichaean Dualism to Early Modern Feminine Redemption develops the historical and genealogical foundation of the trilogy’s wider theory of the Moral Purity Industry. Whereas Volume I analyzes the contemporary moral-commercial regime, Volume II turns to the deeper symbolic grammars through which purity, contamination, hierarchy, absolution, anti-worldliness, and asymmetrical legitimacy became historically intelligible. Its central claim is not that modern institutions simply reproduce medieval doctrine, but that older religious and symbolic structures can survive through mutation, secularization, displacement, and rearticulation. Genealogy is therefore employed as an explanatory method for identifying structured continuity at the level of symbolic grammar rather than institutional sameness. The volume begins with the Manichaean matrix, examining the ontological division of light and darkness, spirit and matter, purity and mixture, and the consequent model of salvation through separation rather than reconciliation. It then follows the transmission and mutation of this dualist-purificatory grammar through Bogomilism and Catharism, including the Interrogatio Iohannis, Cathar cosmology, the Consolamentum, the Servissi, the ritual transmission of prayer, and the Book of the Two Principles. These materials are treated not as disconnected episodes of medieval religious history but as concentrated expressions of a broader grammar of contamination, anti-embodiment, ritual mediation, ontological impurity, authorized absolution, and moral bifurcation. A second major movement examines the relation between women, purity, and the reorganization of authority within dualist and post-dualist formations. The analysis considers female participation and sacramental authority in Catharism, the emergence of the feminized sacred, the destabilization of ordinary sexual and reproductive complementarity under anti-embodied systems of purity, and the development of what the book terms redemptive asymmetry: the increasing association of feminine symbolic status with moral elevation, purity, mediation, and higher legitimacy. The object of analysis is explicitly systemic rather than accusatory; the genealogy concerns archetypes, symbolic valuations, institutionalized asymmetries, and inherited structures of meaning rather than the intentional conduct of women or men as collective agents. The final section traces the early modern transition from sacred feminization to proto-feminist revaluation. Beginning with the Querelle des Femmes, it examines the progressive movement from female dignity and defense toward praise, preeminence, and comparative superiority. Particular attention is given to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Renaissance praise literature, Lucrezia Marinella, and Guillaume Postel, whose writings are interpreted as increasingly explicit articulations of female-centered moral, anthropological, theological, and eventually eschatological hierarchy. Agrippa transforms earlier symbolic elevations into a systematic theology of female preeminence, while Postel projects feminine redemptive centrality onto sacred history and the future itself. Methodologically, the study combines genealogy with philology, semiotics, hermeneutics, cross-textual verification, induction, deduction, and structural comparison. Genealogical claims are tested across related textual strata rather than inferred from isolated resemblance. The volume also employs the Dharma–Theism–Secularism (DTS) axis and the Inversion–Metastasis–Sublimation (IMS) model to explain how symbolic forms can descend from sacred into secular settings while undergoing significant transformation. The result is a model of historical transmission that rejects both crude continuity and total discontinuity. The concluding argument concerns secular residue. The volume proposes that theological structures need not survive as explicit doctrine in order to continue influencing moral perception. Sacred feminization may persist after secularization as evaluative instinct, institutional asymmetry, ideological shorthand, archetypal recurrence, and compressed cultural symbolism. In this framework, modern expressions such as “the future is female” are treated not as direct quotations from earlier sources but as possible archetypal condensations of a much older pattern linking the feminine with moral correction, redemptive centrality, futurity, and legitimacy. The movement traced across the volume is therefore from sacred proximity to redemptive asymmetry, from redemptive asymmetry to female preeminence, from preeminence to historical necessity, and finally from theological structure to secular symbolic residue. Volume II thus supplies the historical depth required by the trilogy’s contemporary social critique. Its purpose is not to reduce the present to the past, but to show how modern systems of moral sorting, symbolic innocence, ideological legitimacy, and purification can become more intelligible when examined against the deeper civilizational grammars from which some of their structural forms may descend.

title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 3
abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume III: Axial Explanation, Secular Mutation, and the Contemporary Regime of Moral Purification completes the trilogy by moving from historical genealogy to systemic explanation, contemporary institutional analysis, and diagnosis. Whereas Volume I identified the Moral Purity Industry as a modern moral-commercial formation and Volume II reconstructed its deeper genealogical antecedents, Volume III asks how older structures of purity, contamination, redemptive asymmetry, and moral bifurcation survive doctrinal rupture and become embedded in secular institutions, markets, professional systems, cultural production, and everyday governance. Its central claim is that the contemporary regime is neither a simple continuation of religious dualism nor a wholly new ideological invention, but the result of descent, mutation, symbolic sedimentation, and institutional recombination. The first section, “The Axial Explanation,” develops the theoretical mechanisms that make this continuity intelligible. The Dharma–Theism–Secularism (DTS) axis explains how sacred and theistic structures descend into cultural, administrative, therapeutic, and commercial forms. The Inversion–Metastasis–Sublimation (IMS) axis explains how these inherited structures change medium and social function without losing their directional grammar. Cognitive Gynocentric Telegony (CGT), ideo-telegony, symbolic imprinting, and collective unconscious residues are then used to account for the persistence of asymmetrical valuations even where direct textual or doctrinal transmission is absent. The contemporary order is consequently interpreted as a form of displaced liturgy: explicit transcendence recedes while structures of guilt, contamination, confession, mediation, absolution, excommunication, and redemption remain socially operative. The second movement examines modern feminism, Marxism, and the purificatory logic of non-reconciliation. The analysis distinguishes systems oriented toward reciprocity and complementarity from those in which one pole becomes increasingly burdened by guilt, suspicion, or historical illegitimacy while another acquires enhanced innocence, authority, or redemptive standing. Marxism is examined as a secular moral-historical structure organized around the abolition of the antagonistic other, while feminism is analyzed in terms of the progressive moral delegitimation of autonomous male legitimacy. The volume introduces gynonormativity as a systemic concept for describing a moral field in which feminine vulnerability, perspective, credibility, and legitimacy increasingly function as normative defaults rather than merely as explicit ideological propositions. A central chapter then analyzes the convergence of feminism and woke capitalism. Rather than treating their apparent opposition as decisive, the book argues that activist moralization, bureaucratic codification, corporate incentives, reputational management, and marketable virtue can become mutually reinforcing. Capitalism provides scale, circulation, institutional infrastructure, and commodification; feminist and progressive moral vocabularies supply categories of injury, purification, legitimacy, and correction. Their convergence is therefore interpreted not primarily as hypocrisy or conscious coordination but as a systemic feature of a hybrid moral-commercial regime in which contradiction itself becomes administratively and economically productive. The volume then turns to The Moral Purity Industry in Practice, examining how symbolic structures become embedded in bureaucracy, social work, law, education, therapy, media, corporate culture, consumer life, and reputational governance. Welfare and professional systems are examined as possible carriers of administratively routinized asymmetry; law as a field in which formal equality may coexist with asymmetrical presumptions and credibility structures; education and therapy as sites of confession, correction, allyship, and permanent self-surveillance; media and film as mechanisms for reproducing the narrative opposition between the pure victim and the contaminating other; and corporate and consumer culture as systems in which virtue itself becomes a visible and purchasable market-sign. Cancel culture and reputational destruction are interpreted as forms of secular excommunication, in which social legitimacy is managed through contamination, disavowal, distancing, and symbolic quarantine. Particular attention is given to the movement from redemptive woman to managed victimhood. The volume argues that earlier forms of feminine sacred and moral centrality can, under secular conditions, be translated into institutional categories of vulnerability, protected status, trauma, credibility, and administratively recognized injury. “Managed victimhood” therefore designates not simply sympathy toward victims, but the transformation of victimhood into an organized moral and bureaucratic position capable of generating authority, intervention, policy, professional mediation, and reputational consequences. The final section, “Diagnosis and Exit,” turns the critique reflexively upon opposition itself. The book argues that resistance frequently strengthens the system when it merely reverses its moral binaries, reproducing an “anti-purity purity” in which enemies, contamination, and symbolic innocence are redistributed rather than transcended. Genuine critique therefore requires more than counter-denunciation. It requires refusal of the shared grammar of moral purification itself. The concluding chapters move from purity toward truth, proportionality, direct judgment, and fallible realism, rejecting both contamination panic and claims to purified innocence. The trilogy culminates in the claim that the Moral Purity Industry represents the late secular consolidation of a much older civilizational scaffold. Structures once articulated metaphysically or theologically now operate through policy, curriculum, therapy, media narratives, compliance systems, branded virtue, consumer identity, and reputational discipline. The contemporary order is thus presented not as a collection of unrelated cultural pathologies but as an integrated and adaptive regime linking woke capitalism, the consumer sexual economy, bureaucratic asymmetry, moralized victimhood, institutional mediation, and symbolic absolution. The work concludes, however, not with a call for reversed moral warfare but with a methodological and ethical alternative. Truth, compassion, direct seeing, proportional judgment, and the acceptance of human fallibility are proposed as alternatives to permanent moral sorting. The stated aim is not to construct a counter-regime of purification, but to weaken the war-form itself by replacing symbolic cleansing with reality-based judgment and by refusing both sentimental falsification and retaliatory dehumanization.

The book argues that resistance frequently strengthens the system when it merely reverses its moral binaries, reproducing an “anti-purity purity” in which enemies, contamination, and symbolic innocence are redistributed rather than transcended. Genuine critique therefore requires more than counter-denunciation. It requires refusal of the shared grammar of moral purification itself. The concluding chapters move from purity toward truth, proportionality, direct judgment, and fallible realism, rejecting both contamination panic and claims to purified innocence. The trilogy culminates in the claim that the Moral Purity Industry represents the late secular consolidation of a much older civilizational scaffold. Structures once articulated metaphysically or theologically now operate through policy, curriculum, therapy, media narratives, compliance systems, branded virtue, consumer identity, and reputational discipline. The contemporary order is thus presented not as a collection of unrelated cultural pathologies but as an integrated and adaptive regime linking woke capitalism, the consumer sexual economy, bureaucratic asymmetry, moralized victimhood, institutional mediation, and symbolic absolution. The work concludes, however, not with a call for reversed moral warfare but with a methodological and ethical alternative. Truth, compassion, direct seeing, proportional judgment, and the acceptance of human fallibility are proposed as alternatives to permanent moral sorting. The stated aim is not to construct a counter-regime of purification, but to weaken the war-form itself by replacing symbolic cleansing with reality-based judgment and by refusing both sentimental falsification and retaliatory dehumanization.

title: GREEK ATHEISM: A REALITY
abstract: This article is a response to Thomas Harrison’s lively thesis that atheism in ancient Greece is not a historical reality but ‘fundamentally, a scholarly mirage’. Repurposing and updating the arguments from the influential work of Lucien Febvre, The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century , Harrison reasons that atheism could not have emerged in the age of Socrates and Plato: all we have from this period are empty accusations of atheism, a religious mentality which was incompatible with total unbelief, and a society in which religion dominated every sphere of personal and public life. This article, conversely, will argue that Greek atheism was a reality: in the fifth century bce and beyond, there were some Athenians who believed in no gods at all. Reasoning from the testimony of atheism in Plato’s Republic and the Laws , and also the intellectual and social conditions of Classical Athens, it will be argued that atheism probably had some limited currency in the upper classes of Athens as a life option. Along the way, the article will assess the merits of applying Febvre’s thesis to an ancient society and identify some of its flaws in the terminological ambiguities it can create.
venue: Greece and Rome

title: Meaning, desire, and the limits of atheism
abstract: Abstract This paper defends a theistic framing of the problem of life’s meaning, albeit one which is intended to be compatible with a kind of naturalism. It makes explicit the significance of desire for an understanding of the issues at hand and draws out some implications for the question of the limits of atheism.
venue: Religious Studies

title: Atheism, evolution, and meaning
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I argue that meaning of the main kinds associated with human life can be described and illuminatingly discussed by atheists who reject all things religious and embrace evolution. Indeed, by considering the different forms evolution can take and with sensitivity to how distinctive meaning-related facts emerge at different stages of macroscale human development and also to the fact that meaning itself evolves, atheists are in a position to show that the evolutionary considerations available to them, rather than an obstacle to a robust and satisfying account of meaning, can be its source.
venue: Religious Studies

title: Scientific atheism in the post-secular context of Perestroika
abstract: The focus of this publication is on the historical fate of scientific atheism at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s. An attempt is made to look at this specific phenomenon of Soviet reality in the context of the theory of the post-secular turn in the late 1970s and 1980s. Historiography has established the opinion that scientific atheism as a whole shared the fate of the entire Soviet system and became a thing of the past in the early 1990s. The researchers propose various approaches to determining the historical conditions and forms of completion of scientific atheism as an ideological project. The minimal attention to the scientific and atheistic discourse of the late 1980s is characteristic. Scientific atheism is considered either as a utopian ideological project of denying religion, or as an artificial administrative and ideological tool, or as an ideologized field of scientific knowledge.The article shows that as a historical phenomenon, scientific atheism was not limited to an ideological project. An appeal to archival sources reflecting internal discussions among atheist ideologists, as well as to publications in scientific atheist publications of the late 1980s, shows that scientific atheism during this period went through a stage of active self-reflection and adaptation to the loss of ideological monopoly and the return of religion to the public space. From this point of view, it has transformed into a specific form of postsecular self-reflexive secularism. The theorists of scientific atheism have managed not only to change the general paradigm of attitudes towards religion – from criticism and denial to its reception and representation for secular society as a universal non-religious ideological platform and expert methodology, but also to identify a gap with bureaucratic and dogmatic administration by the state system.
venue: St Tikhon s University Review

title: Atheism of the Gaps: The Jump from Science to Metaphysics
abstract: This paper introduces "Atheism of the Gaps" as a methodological label for a recurring pattern of reasoning in which a scientific explanation is taken to support a metaphysical conclusion about the non-existence of God. In contrast to "God of the Gaps," where ignorance is used to infer divine action, this paper identifies a symmetrical error: the leap from "we know how" to "therefore God is not." The paper argues that the epistemic success of a scientific explanation does not, by itself, entail any broader metaphysical conclusion. To substantiate this, it distinguishes between scientific, philosophical, and metaphysical levels of explanation, and proposes a principle of epistemic humility as a neutral criterion for evaluating arguments on both sides. The argument is illustrated through the case of junk DNA and debates over biological function, where concepts such as non-functional, useless, suboptimal, and having no role in survival are shown to be conceptually distinct and incapable, without independent argument, of supporting conclusions about design or atheism. The paper further offers a fourfold typology of this error - Functional, Explanatory, Optimization, and Epistemic Gap Atheism - and derives two methodological principles: the insufficiency of scientific explanation and the non-automatic transfer from scientific propositions to metaphysical conclusions. Finally, it specifies conditions under which an argument would not be an instance of this fallacy. The paper concludes that neither theistic nor atheistic metaphysical claims should be regarded as following directly from scientific explanations alone, and that the proposed methodological framework has the potential to be extended to other philosophical and even legal domains.

title: I See Nothing . . . Atheism as the Condition of Credible Theological Grammar
abstract: How can theology maintain credibility when belief in God is optional? This article argues that atheism functions as the existential ground for credible theological grammar in post-Christendom contexts. Examining Tomáš Halík’s recuperation of atheism as ‘impatience with God’ and Emmanuel Falque’s phenomenological treatment of ‘seeing nothing’ as the fundamental human condition, I propose that experiential atheism constitutes theology’s methodological imperative. Grounded in incarnational logic, credible theology must begin with shared finitude rather than transcendent certainties.
venue: Irish Theological Quarterly

title: Два вектора трансформации научного атеизма в его отношении к русскому православию в конце 1980-х годов
abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of archival materials and publications reflecting the complex picture of the transformation of the ideology of scientific atheism at the end of the Soviet era. These processes were associated with the return of the Russian Orthodox Church to the public space of late Soviet society as a significant factor in social development. The opinion about the withdrawal of scientific atheism from the historical arena in connection with the collapse of the ideological system of the USSR has become entrenched in historiography. However, an appeal to sources shows that the ideologists of scientific atheism actively reflected on the changing conditions of public discourse about religion. As a result, two approaches to Russian Orthodoxy have been formulated within the framework of scientific atheism. The first was implemented by theoretical ideologists in the context of a concept called «scientific worldview». Its essence was the recognition of the importance of Orthodoxy as a factor of social development and the reception of its meanings and ideas in a reduced form as an element of secular humanistic ideology. The second approach involved interaction with the church community within the framework of a scientific atheistic paradigm that cuts off the transcendent content of the faith and focuses on cultural and ethical meanings.
venue: Theological Herald

title: TÔM HAI NƯỚC
abstract: Pierre Bao Nguyen is a Franco-Vietnamese-American writer and retired civil engineer. His work explores cosmology, philosophy of science, mathematics, atheism, and intellectual history. He is the author of Cosmology Without Bang, a philosophical inquiry into the limits of cosmic origin and the possibility of thinking the universe without transcendence.

title: New Advances in Cognitive Science of Religion
abstract: ABSTRACT The paper highlights a number of new developments in Cognitive Science of Religion (CSR): It discusses how recent approaches are more mindful of the influence of culture on religious cognition, put more focus on the social role of ritual behavior, and offer explanations for atheism. There is consideration of how new approaches draw insights from other disciplines, especially cognitive neuroscience and computer modeling. Finally, the paper discusses criticisms of some theories and core assumptions.
venue: Religion Compass

title: ‘The Blogger Issue Is Over’ Bangladesh (Sylhet)
abstract: Prologue: Ahmed Rajib Haider, 15 February 2013, Dhaka It was on this date that blogger and activist Ahmed Rajib Haider, known by his pen name Thaba Baba, was hacked to death just outside his home. A leading voice in the Shahbag protests and a sharp critic of Islamist politics, Haider had used his blog to advocate for secular justice and to condemn religious fundamentalism. His murder – not the first attack, but the first in what would become a series of brutal killings – marked a turning point in the public visibility and vulnerability of non-religious dissent. The next day, his coffin was carried in a vast public procession to Shahbag Square, draped in the national flag and accompanied by over 100,000 mourners. However, the act of public grieving became a political flashpoint. Islamist groups seized upon Haider's known atheism to brand the entire movement as nāstik – heretical and immoral. What began as a protest for justice swiftly became a referendum on the legitimacy of atheism in public life, setting in motion a period of heightened risk for secular activists. This chapter returns to the enduring reverberations of that moment – to the quieter and more lasting traces left behind after the spectacle receded. Introduction When I revisited Sylhet for a research stint in February and March 2022, I was warmly welcomed by my former research interlocutors and friends.1 Seeing me again after a long time, some of my atheist interlocutors emphasised, ‘Things are very different from when you came before.’

title: Радянські антирелігійні практики крізь призму вчительських спогадів
abstract: The article analyzes the Soviet public policy of «scientific atheism». The analysis was carried out on the basis of oral historical narratives, archival documents, local history materials. It is noted that in the second half of the 20th century the main way of fighting against religion and the church was mass atheistic propaganda. It was justified by the political doctrine of «scientific atheism» and reinforced by a system of state-administrative pressure. With the help of propaganda, the Soviet intellectual elite created an image of the church as an «internal enemy» in order to use it in the process of forming an imaginary community called the «Soviet people». The territorial boundaries of the publication were delineated by the Lviv, Ternopil and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, on the territories of which the memories were recorded. Attention is given to the textual analysis of memories, which in turn is oriented to the reproduction of the meaning that the teachers placed on their specific life experience today, as well as to the study of the sequence in which the events are arranged in the narrative now, in the present time. It is important in this context to understand the structural difference between what the narrators experienced and what they told, as well as to consider the narrative as containing purely contemporary interpretations and evaluations of the narrators. The article examines how former teachers recall the «struggle against religion», aimed at the atheization of society and their (co)relation to this policy. It describes the involvement of teachers in anti-religious practices which was a sign of the Soviet era, through the organization of educational and educational processes in such a way, to prevent schoolchildren from freely visiting temples or celebrating religious holidays. It was concluded that memories of participation in anti-religious practices reveal a deep psychological discomfort in former teachers, so they resort to psychological defense mechanisms, describing themselves as hostages of their chosen profession, as well as sufficiently formal fulfillment of the requirements of atheist education.
venue: Scientific periodicals of Ukraine

title: Why I Want to Be an Atheist: A Confession of a Reluctant Apologist
abstract: This document serves as a formal declaration and psychological exploration of a profound existential paradox. As a recognized Christian apologist whose work has been validated by both academic and scientific communities, I possess an airtight intellectual conviction of the Christian truth. Yet, I am authoring this preprint to state explicitly that I do not want to be a Christian. I desire the moral void of atheism because it affords the comfort of hedonism without the terror of divine judgment. This paper documents my inability to disprove God, my deep-seated hatred for the restrictive reality of Christianity, and my conscious pursuit of sin over sanctity. I protect truth, not faith, and the truth is horrifying.

title: Why is there no religious Neutrality?!!!
abstract: Why is there no religious Neutrality?!!!The Myth of "Neutrality" and the Illusion of Apathy:Some godless individuals, wishing to shift responsibility away from themselves, love to substitute terms—for instance, calling atheism simply the "absence of belief," although in reality, atheism is a faith in the absence of God in one's heart, of course. An atheist or an agnostic may deny their affiliation with atheists and agnostics, but this is a cheap manipulation. It is merely a mask behind which the godless person hides, denying their involvement to shake off the burden of responsibility and proof. But when they are exposed, they drop their masks!Such "disguised godless individuals" may say: "I am simply non-religious, I don't care (I'm an apatheist)." But from the perspective of truth, this is a fatal, self-deceiving lie:Man is not a mindless robot:Even artificial information systems are built on embedded codes and fundamental principles. Man was created with a spirit, mind, and heart capable of moral choice.Replacing God with an idol:Such godless tricksters who say "I believe in nothing" or "I just don't care" use manipulations to free themselves from responsibility before God. All of this means only one thing: their heart is already occupied by other things (money, comfort, their own ego, the lusts of this world). In first place stands an earthly idol, behind which always stands the ultimate puppet master—the Devil himself, the god of this age, who blinds the minds of unbelievers.As the Apostle Paul wrote in Ephesians (2:2), unbelievers live according to the passions of the flesh, being guided by "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now working in the sons of disobedience.All apatheists, all those who think they are non-religious, or those who are godless yet deny their involvement (though by their actions and views they are godless), are branches of agnosticism. And agnosticism itself is atheism in its pure form. The agnostic says: *"I don't know if God exists."* But in real life, they live as if God does not exist! That means in practice they are 100% atheists. This is merely intellectual cowardice—an attempt to evade responsibility.Where Did Atheism Come From?The entire history of human rebellion against God grows from a single old serpentine fairy tale from Eden:"You will be like gods."Edenic humanism:First, the enemy invited man to put himself in the place of the Creator.Cults and history:This rebellion evolved through the Tower of Babel, the personality cults of Nimrod, the deification of pharaohs in Ancient Egypt (where the concept of God dissolved into abstract forces of nature), and the ancient materialism of Epicurus, who back then was already inventing evolutionary theories and dreaming of unknown worlds. Modern times:Through Jesuit influences, the French Revolution, the rise of pseudo-rationalism, "scientific smoke without science" (scientism), and Darwinism. After Charles Darwin published his godless book On the Origin of Species in 1859, the religious society of England was outraged. But Thomas Huxley (who, by the way, was the first in the world to invent and introduce the term "agnostic" to disguise his unbelief) aggressively rushed into battle, defending the ape-like origin of man.Sitting in his estate, Darwin wrote an official letter to Huxley, where his personal attitude toward his work is recorded in black and white. A direct quote from Darwin's letter: "My dear Huxley... What a man you are! I have read your review in the 'Quarterly.' It is magnificent... You are my good and kind agent for the propagation of the Gospel—that is, the Gospel of the Devil!"(Referring to a book where the true origin of species was nowhere to be found). This document is officially included in the second volume of the academic publication The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (p. 14). The very icon of atheists, Charles Darwin, clearly understood that his theory was not just biology. It was a spiritual anti-biblical weapon, religion inside out, the purpose of which was to erase God, the Creator, and Being from the minds of people.The works of researchers (such as Adrian Desmond in *Huxley: From Devil's Disciple To Evolution's High Priest*) reveal shocking details: Huxley openly stated that his main goal was to destroy the influence of the Church and traditional theology. His lectures about humans descending from apes were called "sermons of the Devil's Gospel" by contemporaries because they brought debauchery, materialism, and nihilism. Marxism, the Paris Commune, Soviet atheism, modern atheist fanatics—all of them serve that same system, often without even realizing they are doing the will of the evil one.Logical Manipulations of the Godless.Many are familiar with atheist manipulations, such as:1.The Category Mistake:They try to measure God—Spirit, who is outside the physical Universe—using physical, laboratory methods suitable only for material objects of creation. But God is not a physical object inside a laboratory; He is the Creator of the laws of physics. We, however, perceive His existence through the unchangeable traces of design (the complexity of information in DNA, RNA, the laws of nature, the moral law in the human heart, and its structured nature).2. The Fallacy of the Absence of Alternatives (the core foundation of atheists, agnostics, and their branches): When scientific data, the laws of logic, and the incredible complexity of living systems (such as the beginning of the Universe or the conditioning of randomness and chaos by physical laws, like the law of conservation of energy and mass) clearly point to an Intelligent Designer (Creator), atheists and agnostics say: "This is not God, we just don't know yet, but someday in the future science will find another explanation." They commit a classic logical fallacy—they use the absence of a proven alternative as the alternative itself! They build their faith on a hypothetical "nothing" in the unfathomable future, solely to escape from the obvious footprint of Divine design.Conclusion:Neutrality does not exist—everyone believes in something, because man was created for God, and if he is not with Christ, he is against Him. All so-called "non-religious," "apatheistic," or "unbiased" positions are merely branches of the single tree of agnosticism and atheism, fueled by the ancient Edenic rebellion. They have no real alternatives, and their "apathy" is merely a protective shell against responsibility before the Holy Judge.
