title: Seven Saints of Science
abstract: This book traces the history of the development of science and religion as pillars of our society and why there is perceived conflict between them. It covers the development of religion in the non-scientific era before the development of science during the Age of Enlightenment, Industrial Revolution, Victorian Era, Age of the New Physics, World War II, and the High Tech Era. The lives of famous scientists with strong beliefs in God are used as examples in each period. This book is important to help stem the rising trend of atheism. It is the only book written from this biographical perspective. One of the co-authors is a prominent physicist with over 40 years of experience and the other is a Christian apologist who is known for writing both non-fiction and fiction Christian books.

title: Personal Prophecy as a ‘Super’natural Ministry: Understanding the Theological Underpinnings of Prophetic Ministry at Bethel Church, Redding, California
abstract: Abstract Anyone who visits Bethel Church, Redding, California, is likely to receive a personal prophecy, either spontaneously or as part of an organised ministry. This study explores Bethel’s prophetic ministry from a practical theological point of view and investigates its theological underpinnings. An important theological theme that emerges is how to understand prophecy as a ‘supernatural ministry’. A key issue is whether the notion of the supernatural as it is presented in Bethel’s teaching and literature is the same as the one embedded in their practice. The notion of supernaturality is discussed in dialogue with James K. A. Smith’s taxonomy of ontological options on the natural-supernatural scale. The study suggests a reworking of Bethel’s philosophical and theological assumptions, moving from an interventionist to a noninterventionist supernaturalism. This would better reflect the spirituality that is implicit in their prophetic practice, and support a theological bulwark against both atheism, panentheism, and deism.
venue: Ecclesial Practices

title: THE ROLE OF RELIGION IN ANTI-COMMUNIST DISCOURSE IN COLD WAR TURKEY AS AN IDEOLOGICAL WEAPON
abstract: This study examines the role of religion in anti-communist discourse in Turkey during the Cold War. It explores how religion-based anti-communist discourse was constructed through the interaction between the international ideological rivalry of the Cold War and Turkey’s historical and political dynamics. The study is based on the works of leading anti-communist authors, publications of the Associations for the Struggle Against Communism, conservative periodicals, and the rhetoric used in anti-communist rallies. Employing qualitative discourse analysis, the research identifies recurring discursive patterns and ideological themes within these texts. The findings demonstrate that communism was constructed as an ontological enemy characterized by atheism and as a threat to moral and social values, while religion functioned as an ideological instrument for social mobilization and for legitimizing criticisms of secularism. The study concludes that religion-based anti-communist discourse in Turkey emerged through the interaction of the global ideological climate of the Cold War with the country’s local political and social dynamics.
venue: Uluslararası Anadolu Sosyal Bilimler Dergisi

title: Preserving Identity Under Totalitarianism: The Adaptation and Resilience of Muslim Communities in the Soviet Union
abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the methods employed by Muslim peoples in the former Soviet Union to preserve their traditional, spiritual, and religious identity under the systemic anti-religious policies, ideological pressures, and repressive measures of the Soviet totalitarian regime. Despite the Soviet authorities' efforts to rapidly secularize society and reshape public consciousness through scientific atheism, the enduring commitment of Muslim communities to their traditional values is clearly demonstrated. The study examines the closure of mosques, the restriction of religious rituals, and the severe obstacles encountered in performing daily worship. Furthermore, it thoroughly explores the role of Sufi brotherhoods as an informal spiritual stronghold. The dialectical relationship between the compromise-oriented policies of official religious directorates on the one hand, and the activities of "parallel mullahs" among the populace on the other, is illustrated. The research findings prove that the Islamic factor during the Soviet era served not merely as a religious belief, but as a primary mechanism for preserving ethnic and national identity.

title: Cambridge Platonism and the Reception of Spinoza in 17th century England
abstract: This article examines the reception of Spinoza’s philosophy in seventeenth-century England, focusing on Henry More and Anne Conway within the circle of the Cambridge Platonists. Taking as its point of departure Spinoza’s claim that the human mind possesses an adequate idea of God which nevertheless often remains inoperative, the paper reconstructs how his immanent monism was interpreted as atheism, enthusiasm, or mysticism. Drawing on the historiographical work of Rosalind Colie (1963) and Sarah Hutton (1984), we revisit the circulation of the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus and the early manuscript versions of the Ethics, arguing that Conway’s Principles constitutes one of the earliest sustained engagements with Spinoza in English. By analyzing More’s defense of divine transcendence and Conway’s reflections on inspiration, imagination, and moral transformation, we show that their critiques implicitly address the operative force of ideas in shaping behavior. The seventeenth-century debate over Spinozism thus anticipates contemporary discussions in the cognitive science of religion concerning imagination, affect, and the regulation of belief.
venue: Revista Archai

title: Being Non-Religious in a Godly Society—Respect and the Negotiation of Social Relations in Indonesia
abstract: This article examines the life of an atheist Chinese Indonesian living in a society where citizens are expected, both legally and socially, to profess belief in God. Occupying a doubly marginalized position as both a member of a historically stigmatized ethnic minority and a non-believer in a religiously defined nation, he must continually negotiate suspicion, belonging, and social acceptance in everyday life. Drawing on a Goffmanian framework and a biographical study of one individual, the article explores how different forms of stigma generate different strategies of management. While visible ethnic difference requires responses to actual stigmatization, atheism remains a concealable but potentially more consequential source of moral suspicion. The analysis shows how these intersecting stigmas are navigated through practices of adjustment, passing, and anticipatory self-presentation. In particular, it identifies the local practice of hormat (respect) as a key moral orientation through which social relationships are maintained despite difference. Attention to hormat reveals how people may navigate stigma as a deeply social and historically shaped condition through practices that prioritize relational harmony and recognition of others’ agency.
venue: Entangled Religions

title: ҚАЗАҚ ДАЛАСЫНДАҒЫ ИШАНДАР МЕН МОЛДАЛАР ЖӘНЕ ОЛАРДЫҢ КЕҢЕС ӨКІМЕТІ ТАРАПЫНАН ҚУДАЛАУҒА ҰШЫРАУЫ
abstract: In this work, the role of ishans and mullahs in the religious and social life of the Kazakh steppe in the pre-Soviet and early years is considered, as well as the policy of persecution of priests by the Soviet authorities is analyzed. At the beginning of the twentieth century, ishans and mullahs played a key role in the spread of Islam among Kazakhs, as well as were important figures in the organization of public life, education and culture. However, with the establishment of Soviet power, an active campaign was launched to abolish religious institutions, which also affected the Muslim clergy. The Soviet authorities promoted atheism and organized repressions against the ishans and mullahs, demanding the abolition of all religious manifestations. These actions included arrest, deportation, shooting, and other forms of violence. As a result, a significant number of religious leaders were destroyed or forced to emigrate. Repression led to the destruction of the traditional religious structure and profound changes in the life of the Kazakh people. The work also analyzed the consequences of this persecution for Kazakh society, culture and religious practice and stressed the importance of studying this period in order to understand the historical context of religious and social changes in Kazakhstan in the twentieth century.

title: Samuel Beckettas Rough for Theatre I and II: A Revolt against Absurdity
abstract: Deemed as depictions of dejection intermingled with penetrative multiaccentuality, nothingness, and murkiness, Beckett's multilayered texts lead the mind of the reader/observer into a deadlock in rendering a plausible connotation camouflaged in their sub-texts. As a result, the paradoxical and baffling amalgamation of simplicity and complexity in his works keeps the readers and pundits captivated in the fanciful web of the text. Expectedly, this delusive feature has tantalized a bumper crop of articles to mark Beckett down as a paragon of absurdism and atheism over the past few decades. However, by ploughing new fields and charting new territories of his works, we can redefine and re-delineate Beckett's ideologies as non-absurdist and theist and ultimately he himself as an absurdistic writer rather than an absurdist author. Contrary to the mainstream impression of hermeneutists about Beckett's rationalizations that are fallaciously thought to be absurd and purposeless, his argumentations of absurdity are not a stymie to propagandize absurdism, but an initiative to actuate our consciousness to eschew our absurd life in order to lead us to a new sphere of reality and meaning. Therefore, this paper is to underpin the above-mentioned avowals by re-introducing Beckett as a crusader against absurdity and mental stagnation through a comparative review of Rough for Theatre I and II.
venue: Global Journal of Human-Social Science

title: Revisiting Marx’s Critique of Religion in the Post-Secular Age: A Critical Philosophical Analysis
abstract: The article revisits the critique of religion by Karl Marx in a critical philosophical perspective by both addressing the traditional understandings and current post-secular discourse. Though Marx is often characterized as having described religion as the opium of the people, this paper will point to the fact that, a more nuanced interpretation of his corpus, however, demonstrates that his dialectic is more nuanced than either the crude atheism or the political theology that he is said to have identified is able to offer. Relying on recent work by Hammer (2025), Vizcaiando (2024) and others, I would argue that the materialist critique of religion by Marx cannot be detached and disassociated with his larger social change agenda. But I also see a lot of philosophical contradictions in the stand of Marx, especially his inability to explain the existence of religious phenomena even in the post-revolutionary situations. This paper explores the need to supplement but not abandon the critique developed by Marx based on recent work by Habermas (2008), Žižek (2012), and Eagleton (2016). I suggest that religion is also ideological mystification and a reservoir of utopian wish a duality that, Marx acknowledged but not theorized. The paper concludes that a re-formed Marxist perspective on religion needs to drop any teleological notions concerning secularization and preserve the materialist emphasis on seeking to map religious consciousness into its socio-economic origins.

title: A Unified Definition of Realism The Denial of Fate as the Condition of Explicability and Intervention
abstract: Realism recurs across historiography, political theory, literary criticism, and socialscience methodology, yet no existing account identifies what generates it as anintellectual attitude across these domains. This paper proposes a unified definition:realism is the acceptance of the absence of divine will in the causal explanation ofempirical events. So defined, realism is not a set of claims about the world but atransformation applied to explanatory structures—one that simultaneously producestwo conditions: the explicability of outcomes (because immanent causes can beanalyzed) and the possibility of intervention (because immanent causes can be actedupon). The definition is not atheism; it brackets divine intention from empiricalcausation while leaving the metaphysical question of God's existence untouched. Theverb "acceptance" rather than "exclusion" marks a crucial distinction: the realist doesnot expel the gods but recognizes that they were never present in the causal chain. Thepaper demonstrates this operation across four canonical cases—Thucydides,Machiavelli, Flaubert, and Weber—and derives from the definition a diagnosticreversal test: any explanatory structure that is transcendent, opaque, and foreclosesintervention reinstates fate under a secular name. General equilibrium in economics,the p-value threshold in statistics, and the anthropic principle in cosmology are shownto exhibit this structure. Realism, on this account, is not a doctrine of resignation butthe structural precondition for intervention—a permanent task rather than a completedachievement.

title: Historical context, Islam, and ethnic culture in the religious identification of ethnoterritorial groups of Tatars
abstract: This article presents the findings of a study of ethnoreligious identification among Tatars residing in Siberia and the Republic of Crimea. The study aims to identify and analyze the impact of several key factors, namely: a) the effect of the socio-political environment on the specific features of ethnoreligious identification within these groups; b) the influence of the ethnic group’s social history on the interlinking of ethnic culture and Islam in identification processes; c) the role of codifying agents, including the state; d) the impact of Islamic globalization. The study is grounded in a secondary analysis of data from ethnosociological investigations into Tatar identity, conducted in Tyumen, the Tyumen Region, and the Republic of Crimea in 2016–2019. Some of these materials have been previously used and published earlier by the author. In conclusion, it is necessary to highlight the significance of Russian historical conditions — in particular, the Soviet-era institutionalization, which fostered the integration of elements of ethnic culture with Islamic practices. State support for national cultures contributed to the emergence of “folk” Islam. Through the mechanism of familial transmission of religious values, this phe-nomenon helped sustain ethnoreligious identification among the studied Tatar groups amid the officially promoted atheism of the Soviet period. Furthermore, the pronounced entanglement of ethnic identity and Islamic practices revitalized the discourse surrounding “traditional” Islam in the context of post-Soviet re-Islamization in Russia. This dynamic continues to shape the religious identification of Muslim Tatars today.

title: The Carlo Compendium of Cognitive Geometries: A Unified Dynamical‑Systems Atlas of Belief, Non‑Belief, Anti‑Belief, Parody‑Belief, and Non‑Geometry States
abstract: This compendium presents the first complete Carlo‑mathematical mapping of cognitive stances as dynamical systems within a unified multi‑basin manifold. Across twelve fully modelled architectures—atheism, agnosticism, ignosticism, apatheism, deism, SBNR, secular humanism, existentialism, absurdism, Jediism, Pastafarianism, and the No‑Label stance—the work demonstrates that belief systems are not identities but **geometric behaviours** defined by attractor depth, drift freedom, entropy variability, and compression regimes. Each stance is expressed through: - **Attractor geometry** - **Drift vectors** - **Entropy profiles** - **Compression structures** - **Transition dynamics** - **Occlusion boundaries** The result is a complete cognitive manifold where open‑structure, suspended‑structure, semantic‑indeterminate, low‑activation, single‑anchor, symbolic‑cluster, ethical‑compression, identity‑compression, dual‑attractor, mythic‑ethical, satirical‑structured, and non‑geometry states coexist within a single deductive field. At the centre of the compendium lies the Carlo Closure Equation, summarising the entire manifold: \[\text{Cognitive State} = f(A_d, D_f, E_v, C_r)\] Where: - \(A_d\) = attractor depth - \(D_f\) = drift freedom - \(E_v\) = entropy variability - \(C_r\) = compression regime Each stance is a unique solution to this function. The No‑Label stance forms the special case: \[\text{Cognitive State}_{\text{No‑Label}} = f(\varnothing)\] The only configuration where all parameters collapse into **non‑structure**, defining the boundary of the manifold while existing outside it. This compendium concludes with a unified Carlo deduction: > **Belief systems are geometries. > They are not answers but attractor configurations. > They are not categories but dynamical behaviours.** And the stance with no label, no clue, no mention, and no definition simply: is what it is. Includes an interactive HTML visualiser rendering the full 13-stance Carlo Cognitive Manifold in infinite space with live entropy flux, vector transition dynamics, and telemetry inspection—which also nearly killed my sweet sweet Lenovo laptop whilst I cooked it. title: ‘I Call Being an Atheist a Convert’ Europe (Sweden and the Netherlands)
abstract: Prologue: Ananta Bijoy Das, April–May 2015, Embassy of Sweden, Dhaka and Sylhet Ananta Bijoy Das was a science writer and editor based in Sylhet, in northeastern Bangladesh. He edited Jukti (Logic), a quarterly science magazine, and founded the Sylhet Science and Rationalist Council. Through his writing and public engagement, he sought to popularise scientific thinking and secular humanist ideas in a social context where such positions were marginal and increasingly dangerous. He also contributed regularly to Mukto-Mona (Free Mind), a Bengali-language online platform associated with free thought, atheism and rationalist critique. Much of his work focused on biological evolution and on challenging religious orthodoxies, including aspects of both Islam and Hinduism. By 2013, Das's name had begun to circulate on assassination lists linked to Islamist extremist groups. He received repeated threats, and the risk to his safety was well known within international writer and human rights networks. In early 2015, he was accepted for a placement through the International Cities of Refuge Network (ICORN) and invited by Swedish PEN to travel to Sweden to speak publicly about the escalating violence against secular writers in Bangladesh. Despite this, and despite the documented threats against him, the Swedish embassy in Dhaka refused his visa application in April 2015. The decision stated that he belonged to a category of applicants considered likely not to leave the Schengen area, and that the purpose of his visit was not sufficiently urgent.

title: Повсякденне життя школярів західних областей УРСР в умовах радянізації (1944–1953)
abstract: The article examines the everyday life of schoolchildren in the western regions of the USSR in 1944–1953 in the context of intensive Sovietization of the region. Based on archival materials, published sources, and scientific works, the social, material, everyday, and ideological factors of the functioning of school education in the postwar period are identified. The impact of the difficult socio-political situation on the situation of students, as well as the contradictions of the Soviet educational policy, are analyzed in detail. Special attention is paid to the transformation of the content of education in the Western Ukrainian region in accordance with all-Union standards, the introduction of an ideological and political component in education, and the displacement of national educational traditions. The role of the school as one of the main instruments for forming loyalty to the Soviet regime is investigated. The activities of pioneer and Komsomol organizations, methods of their influence on students' leisure time, and real practices of functioning, which were often forced, are characterized. The influence of the Ukrainian national underground on school life, its attempts to counteract Soviet ideological expansion and preserve the national direction of youth education are highlighted. It is emphasized that the post-war life of schoolchildren in the western regions of the USSR was characterized by difficult material and living conditions, a shortage of teachers and educational materials. It is argued that Soviet educational policy sought to form a materialistic worldview, atheism and loyalty to the authorities through curricula, the activities of communist organizations and students' leisure, but the effectiveness of ideological influence was limited due to the resistance of youth and the struggle of the Ukrainian underground. It is concluded that the everyday life of schoolchildren in 1944–1953 was formed under the influence of a number of factors, which resulted in a complex and contradictory everyday reality.

title: ‘I Crossed an Invisible Line’ Introduction
abstract: • Dhaka, Bangladesh – 13 February 2013: Secular activist Ahmed Rajib Haider is stabbed, allegedly in retaliation for his outspoken criticism of religion. His death becomes a turning point in the public contestation of atheism, secularism and Islam in Bangladesh. • Multan, Pakistan – 13 March 2013: University lecturer Junaid Hafeez is accused of blasphemy by Islamist students for allegedly defiling the Prophet's name on social media. A year later, his lawyer is shot dead. In 2019, Hafeez is sentenced to death. Appeal remains ongoing. • Pune, India – 20 August 2013: Rationalist leader Dr Narendra Dabholkar is assassinated while on his morning walk. Right-wing Hindu nationalists, with reported links to the hardline group Sanatan Sanstha, are suspected of orchestrating the attack. • Sylhet, Bangladesh – 12 May 2015: Writer and activist Ananta Bijoy Das is killed after being denied a temporary visa that would have allowed him to seek asylum in Sweden. His murder has significant repercussions for the Swedish asylum system, creating a brief period in which a growing number of atheists and secular activists from Bangladesh gain protection. International humanist and rationalist organisations intensify their lobbying around asylum and protection in response to the killings. In 2013 and the years that followed, a series of targeted attacks unfolded across South Asia, attributed to both militant Islamist and Hindu nationalist actors. While many were decentralised acts by radicalised individuals, others bore the imprint of state actors or proceeded with forms of tacit state involvement.

title: LIFE WITHOUT GOD A Philosophy of Survival, Meaning, Freedom, and Human Flourishing
abstract: Life Without God: A Philosophy of Survival, Meaning, Freedom, and Human Flourishing examines one of the most enduring questions of human existence: how should we live if belief in God is not treated as a necessary foundation for morality, meaning, or purpose? Beginning with the origins of religion and human belief, the book explores evolution, cultural development, social institutions, the philosophical arguments for and against the existence of God, and the possibility of constructing an ethical life without divine command. Rather than presenting atheism as a final answer, the book adopts a naturalistic and self-correcting approach in which conclusions remain open to evidence, criticism, and revision. At the center of the work is Survival Philosophy, a framework built around truth-seeking, corrigibility, contextual judgment, sustainable survival, human flourishing, reciprocal freedom, cooperation, integrity, adaptability, and intentional living. The book argues that survival alone is not enough. A life worth preserving must also contain freedom, knowledge, meaningful relationships, creativity, justice, personal growth, and the possibility of improvement. Rejecting both rigid dogmatism and simplistic moral relativism, Life Without God proposes a philosophy designed for imperfect human beings living under uncertainty. Its central message is that the absence of absolute certainty need not lead to meaninglessness. Instead, it can increase our responsibility to think carefully, cooperate intelligently, revise our mistakes, and build conditions in which worthwhile forms of life can continue. Ultimately, this book is not merely about whether God exists. It is about a deeper question: Given the knowledge available to us, the freedom we can build, and the finite time we possess, what kind of life—and what kind of world—is worth creating?

title: Islamic Epistemology from Al-Buti’s Perspective: Criticism of Positivism in the Preface to the Book of Kubra al Yaqiniyyat al Kawniyyah
abstract: This research is motivated by the hegemony of Western materialistic positivist epistemology, which reduces science to the empirical realm, triggers an epistemological crisis, and delegitimizes metaphysical truths. The study addresses how Shaykh M. Said Ramadhan Al-Buti’s Islamic epistemology critiques materialistic positivism and evaluates its methodology as an effective antithesis. The objectives are to analyze Al-Buti’s manhaj ilmi, evaluate his critique of positivism, assess its methodological effectiveness, and outline its implications for contemporary Islamic theology in counteracting atheism. The framework relies on Al-Buti’s integrative epistemology, synergizing the senses (al-hiss), reason (al-’aql), and valid news (al-khabar al-sadiq) to achieve certainty (al-yaqin). Employing a qualitative literature study with philosophical-epistemological, historical-sociological, and dialectical-critical approaches, the primary data source is the Preamble of Kubra al-Yaqiniyyat al-Kawniyyah, supported by secondary literature on science philosophy. Data collected via critical reading and proposition extraction were analyzed using descriptive-analytical, comparative, and dialectical-critical methods. Results demonstrate that Al-Buti’s manhaj ilmi rejects the reason-revelation dichotomy by establishing proportional standards of proof based on the object’s nature (empirical for physical matter; analytical-transmissive for metaphysics). His critique successfully falsifies positivism by exposing internal contradictions within its verification principles and taxonomic reductions. Critical reflection reveals that despite suspending qiyas mantiqi, Al-Buti’s methodology remains a highly effective counter to modern positivism. Its implications offer a philosophical resolution refuting scientism and establishing a sound argumentative foundation for faith education. In conclusion, Islamic theology possesses an independent, objective scientific methodology that dismantles Western positivism's monopoly on truth while restoring the authority of revelation and reason.
venue: Jurnal Iman dan Spiritualitas

title: Thoughts on the Book Production, Usage, and the French Language in Egodocumental Letters of Reverend Remigian Kossakowski (1730–1780)
abstract: This article is a case study that presents an opinion on book production and trade, as well as the importance of the language in which the book is printed, as expressed in the ego documentary correspondence created in the late Enlightenment. The data come from the letters, written by a former Jesuit priest in Hrodna and Vilnius, a former Professor at Vilnius University, Remigian Korwin Kossakowski. Kossakowski sent letters from Paris to Vilnius, where he worked as a representative of the Commission of National Education of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (PLC), in addressing his colleague, a former confrere Jesuit and former teacher, Marcin Odlanicki Poczobut. Close, friendly relations with the addressee may explain the egodocumentality and a certain intimacy in Kossakowski’s letters; this very reason allowed Kossakowski to freely express his thoughts and elaborate on topics relevant to him. Among other things, Kossakowski discussed the role of language as a medium of a particular worldview. He also compared book production and usage in Paris and in Vilnius. While preaching against the French language as a channel through which atheism and libertinism could easily spread, Kossakowski seemingly repeated the clichés found in some Lithuanian sermons and Polish texts of the epoch. At the same time, he expressed sympathy and pride in his vernacular (Polish) and ideas of peculiarity of every nation’s mind, thus somewhat resembling the thoughts of his contemporary, Johann Gottfried Herder. Kossakowski disapproved of the global dominance of French, achieved at the expense of weaker languages, such as Polish. He criticized the poor quality of the abundant, hastily prepared French publications, while blaming his compatriots for being too lazy and not self-assured enough to write original books. Kossakowski’s outspoken position is a rare testimony, which is valuable for the history of mentalities in the PLC. The article builds on the analysis of Kossakowski’s correspondence from 1777 to 1780, parts of which the author has previously discussed in international conferences.

title: RE-EXPLORING HARDY’S PURPORTED PESSIMISM FROM JUNGIAN PERSPECTIVE
abstract: Thomas Hardy is one of the last novelists of the Later Victorian Period. Being a versatile and prolific writer, he tried his hand at writing poetry, short story, and novel successfully. Having read the works of agnostic and atheistic philosophers, he developed a belief that there is some malevolent, hostile and vindictive cosmic force that is determined to oppose man. This force is relentlessly committed to frustrating his plans and schemes. He opines that this antagonistic force is ill-disposed and inimical to those in particular who assert their authority and want to get their own way. This belief made Thomas Hardy produce a copious amount of work speaking of his pessimistic perspective on life, rendering him conspicuous for critics and expositors. This research paper aims to re-explore the purported doom and gloom in Hardy’s works from Jungian viewpoint. That is to say, this delve is an endeavor to ascertain the cause of his literary pessimism, employing a lens what Carl Gustav Jung conceives as "The Shadow." As regards the trail of pessimism in Thomas Hardy's literary endeavors, countless volumes of primary and secondary body of knowledge apropos of matter have been delved deep into, involving his autobiography, biographies, and critical commentaries written on his works. A meticulous read of these volumes has led to the discovery that Hardy's perusal of the leaves of the works of his contemporary English Naturalist Charles Darwin, the gloomy Teutons Eduard van Hartman and Arthur Schopenhauer and Greek tragedians, Shakespeare and his contemporary agnostics impacted Hardy's spiritual and moral compass. Critics believe that pessimism, agnosticism, and atheism originating from The Victorian Intellectual Revolution caused Thomas Hardy to become pessimist, determinist, fatalist, agnostic and ultimately atheist viewing life, religion, universe and God in a pessimistic light. Furthermore, other elements that triggered his pessimism, involve circumstances of his intimate life, to be exact, his ephemeral yet amorous alliance with his betrothed Tryphena Sparks, and his failed marriage with his first wife Emma Lavinia Gifford. The pessimism resulting from Hardy's study of the works of all the aforementioned contemporaries, religious intellectuals, German philosophers, the influence of scientific development, and his failed intimate relationships with the aforementioned two women, became repressed in his unconscious, which later on manifested itself in his works such as Jude the Obscure and A Pair of Blue Eyes featuring people, their state of affairs, their faith resonating with Hardy himself, his own life circumstances, his own religious beliefs and with that of those associated with him in real life. In plain, this paper establishes it for a fact that literary Naturalism and Antihumanism of Thomas Hardy is inextricable from his personal and philosophical doctrine manifesting itself in the Magnum opus, unbeknownst to Hardy.

title: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century
abstract: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century An Agnostic Enlightenment for the Twenty-First Century What remains when inherited certainty begins to fade? For centuries, religious institutions shaped morality, identity, law, and humanity's understanding of existence. Yet the twenty-first century presents an unprecedented reality: scientific progress, democratic institutions, neuroscience, psychology, and universal access to information have profoundly transformed how people approach truth, authority, and belief. In The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century, Northon Salomão de Oliveira offers a bold yet balanced philosophical exploration of this historic transition. Rather than celebrating atheism or defending traditional religion, the book proposes a third path: agnosticism as an intellectual discipline, grounded in evidence, epistemic humility, and the enduring values of the Enlightenment. Drawing inspiration from Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Baron d'Holbach, Karl Popper, Steven Pinker, A. C. Grayling, Martha Nussbaum, Jürgen Habermas, and other influential thinkers, this work examines the decline of religious authority while recognizing the enduring psychological, cultural, and ethical roles that religion has played throughout civilization. Inside, readers will discover: * Why religious dogma is gradually losing its monopoly over truth. * How science, philosophy, and democratic institutions are reshaping moral authority. * The psychological functions religion still fulfills, even in secular societies. * Why agnosticism may represent the most intellectually honest position in an age of uncertainty. * How dogmatic thinking survives beyond religion through ideology, politics, and digital culture. * The unfinished project of building meaning, community, and ethical responsibility without unquestioned authority. Blending philosophy, psychology, history, political theory, cognitive science, and cultural criticism, this book invites readers to confront one of the defining questions of our age: Can humanity preserve meaning, morality, and human dignity after the decline of unquestioned religious authority? Provocative, deeply researched, and written with literary elegance, The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century is an invitation to rethink belief, embrace intellectual honesty, and participate in the continuing Enlightenment of the modern world. This is not a book against faith. It is a book in favor of reason, freedom of inquiry, and the courage to live with honest uncertainty. title: Works for 8/10/2026 - Bob Ross
abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/b1bf2b8a-9ce8-440e-ba76-8f8c1e29a6fd?authuser=1 Light from Light: Invariance, Negative Time, and the Relational Structure of Reality develops a cross-disciplinary account of reality organized around a simple question: when representations change across observers, frames, channels, histories, and scales, what remains stable enough to identify one underlying reality? Beginning with Genesis 1 and the narrative priority of light before the luminaries, the paper moves through classical optics, electromagnetism, quantum field theory, special relativity, general relativity, gravitational lensing, astronomy, memory, and the problem of time in quantum gravity. Across these domains it identifies a recurring relational grammar of source, propagation, transformation, local reception, differential accessibility, and invariant constraint. Different representations need not imply different realities; lawful transformations can preserve sufficient structure for one source, event, or system to remain reconstructable across multiple receivers. The paper introduces negative time as a receiver-relative temporal convention in which a later resolved state is assigned coordinate zero and earlier unfinished states receive negative coordinates relative to that completion. This does not imply retrocausation, backward information transfer, or reversal of physical time. Instead, it formalizes the fact that later receiver states can possess more resolved history and therefore interpret earlier states differently without physically altering those earlier events. Biblical and Qur’anic light traditions are then subjected to prospective testing. If light functions as a recurring grammar of accessibility, passages concerning revelation, guidance, blindness, recognition, disclosure, judgment, resurrection, and fulfillment should disproportionately cluster around light, sight, darkness, and related language. Genesis, Isaiah, John, Paul, Revelation, and the Qur’an repeatedly instantiate this predicted structure. The Nicene formula “Light from Light” is then examined as a dense theological compression preserving origin, distinction, shared divine nature, generation rather than creation, and unity without division. The paper subsequently returns to Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas. The Unmoved Mover and First Cause are distinguished from the earliest event in a temporal sequence. Classical natural theology instead asks after the non-derived ground of actuality upon which the entire created causal order depends. God is therefore not identified with a photon, electromagnetic field, spacetime event, or temporal endpoint. Physics describes transformations within an actual intelligible order; First Cause reasoning asks why such an order is actual at all. Later sections apply the same source-receiver framework to communication between human beings and artificial intelligence through the recurring operation receive, flutter, resolve, transmit. The paper argues that relation cannot be treated merely as a decorative property added after independently complete entities are already understood. Human beings, artificial systems, physical fields, institutions, memories, and communities can function as coherent relational unities at one scale while containing extensive internal multiplicity at another. The central conclusion is that there is one reality, many receivers, many partial representations, and recoverable invariants. Relation carries information, history, identity, and participation across changing frames, channels, temporal positions, and descriptive scales. Physical light provides the clearest demonstration because it carries information, reveals distant history locally, structures causal accessibility, undergoes transformation through matter and geometry, and remains governed by invariant relativistic constraints. The appendices include a full plain-language explanation for younger readers, a biography of Bob Ross, a formal derivation of the paper’s invariant-relational argument, and an extended analysis of artificial intelligence, atheism, and apologetics as a problem of reproducible reasoning audit rather than rhetorical persuasion.

title: Rationality and Truth
abstract: According to Margaret Cavendish, there is a rational “part” to all material things—including rocks, plants, cats, and humans. Alternatively, they all have some “degree” of reason.1 The philosophy of value that I will unearth in this book does not depend on this controversial generalization. It is consistent with Cavendish’s aesthetics and ethics that only some material things—humans and cats, say, but not rocks and plants—are rational. Nevertheless, what Cavendish understands by rationality—at least in humans and other animals—is important for expounding and assessing her reflections on value. How so? For one thing, Cavendish holds that the responses of creatures like ourselves to values and to disvalues—the thoughts and feelings they occasion—are rational responses.2 For another, she holds that rational responses—and motions of the rational part of matter more generally—are themselves among the bearers of value and of disvalue.3 I will unpack these ideas later in the book. The aim of the present chapter is to prepare the ground for doing so. Accordingly, I will start by asking what, for Cavendish, is distinctive of the rational part of matter (§3.2). How does it differ from the other parts—the sensitive and the inanimate—and why do its distinguishing features justify the application of the label ‘rational’? The standard answer to such questions appeals to the freedom with which the rational part moves. After arguing that that answer is incomplete, I will consider two ways of supplementing it. The first, I will argue, lacks textual support (§3.3). The second is my alternative (§3.4). The resultant proposal is that the rational part of matter is properly so-called because its motions are free and stand in a teleological relation to the truth. Addressing some objections to this proposal—both exegetical and substantive—will serve as an opportunity to add further details (§3.5). With Cavendish’s conception of rationality in full view, I will note respects in which it is similar to but also different from that of her contemporary, René Descartes (§3.6). I will then compare both Cavendish’s and Descartes’ conceptions to their Aristotelian and Stoic precursors. It counts in favour of my reading that it reveals Cavendish’s reflections on reason, like those of Descartes, to draw on ancient thought with which she was undoubtedly familiar, albeit at some remove (see §1.5). As Cavendish should be the first to admit, “nothing is created anew, which never was in Nature before.”4 Before proceeding to the main discussion, I will make some preliminary points. The question is: In virtue of what does some part of matter qualify as rational? More straightforwardly, in what does rationality consist? As stated, the question is ambiguous. Cavendish distinguishes two senses of ‘rational’—the “philosophical” and the “vulgar.”5 This is the distinction between being subject to standards of rationality and meeting them, respectively, or between having rational capacities and successfully exercising them. Rational in the philosophical sense contrasts with arational; rational in the vulgar sense contrasts with irrational.6 For Cavendish, arational means sensitive or inanimate. In the first instance, I will explain what it takes to be rational in the vulgar sense. Cavendish’s answer to this, it turns out, immediately provides an answer to the question of what it takes to be rational in the philosophical sense. As noted in §2.5, Cavendish restricts her account of sensory perception as “patterning” to animals, sometimes to humans. In a similar fashion, Cavendish is explicit that the rationality of humans and other animals differs from that of non-animals, given the differences in their “exterior and interior figures.”7 She writes: A Stone has Reason [ . . . ]; but yet it has not animal or humane [ . . . ] reason, because it is not of animal kind; but being a Mineral, it has Mineral [ . . . ] reason.8 In line with this, I will present what I take to be Cavendish’s account of animal—or, more cautiously, human—rationality. title: Proof of the Existence of God (in Russian)
abstract: Based on a new system of metaphysical categories developed by the author in his work «The Metaphysics of the True» [1], an analysis is conducted of the concept of God as ultimate existence. The necessity of a source of existence for anything as the MEANING of a timeless and spaceless contradiction the impossibility of absolute Nothingness is demonstrated. Space and time are presented as forms of interpretation of existence. The limitations of arguments based on traditional metaphysics of being and the existent are demonstrated. An analysis is conducted of basic Christian ideas as representations of the form of limit-existing MEANING На основании новой системы метафизических категорий, разработанной автором в его работе «Метафизика достоверного» [1], произведён анализ понятия Бога как предельного существования. Показана необходимость источника существования чего-либо как СМЫСЛА вневременного и внепространственного противоречия невозможности абсолютного Ничто. Пространство и время представлены как формы интерпретаций существования. Показана ограниченность доказательств основанных на традиционной метафизике бытия и сущего. Произведён анализ базовых христианских идей как репрезентации формы предельно существующего СМЫСЛА.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The ontological argument in the philosophical theology of Bernhardt Welte: a way of the reading of Anselm
abstract: The ontological proof of the existence of God was formulated by Anselm of Canterbury in the 11th century and remains controversial throughout the history of philosophy. In the 20th century, philosophers began to turn to him especially often, which is associated with the active development of scientific thought. Anselm's argument began to be interpreted, criticized, and challenged in such fields of thought as logical research, phenomenology, and Protestant neo-orthodoxy. One of such philosophers, for whom the ontological argument became an important point of consideration within his own philosophical thought, was the Catholic theologian Bernhardt Welte (1906-1983), who turned to the legacy of Anselm as part of his phenomenological project of knowledge of God, which became part of a more general project - the renewal of traditional Catholic metaphysics. At the same time, the issue of rational justification of the existence of God remains an independent and always relevant issue for Christian theological thought, within which the ontological argument of Anselm of Canterbury is one of the most original and significant attempts at such justification. In our research, we aimed to consider not only the role and function of the ontological argument in the work of B. Welte, but also the peculiar revival of Anselm's argument in the philosophical theology of the 20th century using the example of the chosen philosopher. This choice is due to the fact that, in our opinion, Welte presented one of the most extensive and original systems of the knowledge of God (he called it “The project of the ways of the knowledge of God"), combining the phenomenological method with traditional Catholic metaphysics. In this sense, Welte is not only a follower of the tradition of Catholic theology, going back to the second half of the 20th century through neo-scholasticism and neotomism, but also a thinker of “his” time, close to the phenomenology and fundamental ontology of Heidegger.
venue: St Tikhon s University Review

title: SIMILARITAS KONSEP PEMIKIRAN THOMAS AQUINAS DALAM PANDANGAN FILSAFAT JAWA SERAT WIRID HIDAYAT JATI
abstract: This article discusses the Thomism concept of thought initiated by Thomas Aquinas and the divinity views contained in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati by Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito as well as the interference of the beliefs or religions held by Thomas Aquinas and Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito. The aim of writing this article is to find out the similarities between the divinity and cosmological concepts of Thomas Aquinas and the concept of divinity in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati by Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito and the theological views of both. The research method in this study is the literature study method. The result of this research is the finding of similarities between the thoughts of Thomas Aquinas and Ronggowarsito as outlined in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati and the influence of religion in the perspectives of Thomas Aquinas and Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito. The similarities are in the existence of God, the oneness of God, cosmological arguments and the creation theory of the universe. The religious influence that interferes in Thomas Aqinas' view is Christianity, while in Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito's view is Islam.
venue: SOSFILKOM Jurnal Sosial Filsafat dan Komunikasi

title: Personal Ultimate Ground: An Independently Developed Philosophical-Formal Framework
abstract: This dossier presents an independently developed philosophical-formal framework for a Personal Ultimate Ground (PUG). The project separates formally checkable modal consequences from substantive metaphysical premises, constructs an explicit impersonal counter-model, and audits the inferential bridges connecting grounding, normativity, agency, reason-responsiveness, sourcehood and ultimacy. The principal model is presented as an abductive explanatory proposal rather than as a deductive proof of the existence of God. A separate single-premise benchmark assumes U* = ◇□P and shows that, under S5, ◇□P entails □P and hence P. The benchmark is deliberately classified as conditional because U* itself is not established. The dossier therefore makes a narrower and more defensible claim: the Personal Ultimate Ground is proposed as a potentially superior unifying explanation among the models examined, while the decisive metaphysical bridge excluding an adequate impersonal ground remains unproved.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Do Americans Believe in the Afterlife? A Machine Learning Approach
abstract: Belief in the afterlife has held profound significance for humanity since time immemorial, influencing how individuals contemplate mortality, meaning, and legacy. The current study aimed to identify key factors that predict belief in the afterlife and to examine whether there is a connection between religious identification and such belief. The analysis was based on data from the General Social Survey, spanning 2006 to 2022. A Random Forest model was employed, incorporating multiple imputations and Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique for sampling. Here we show that the key variables associated with belief in the afterlife are the respondent's age, frequency of prayer, and confidence in the existence of God. Notably, the results suggest that belief in the afterlife is more strongly associated with general religiosity than with affiliation to any specific religious tradition. While belief in the afterlife varies across individuals and cultures, it remains crucial for understanding how people cope with mortality and how death and the prospect of an afterlife are perceived within societal contexts.
venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)

title: Philosophical Theology: The Basics
abstract: What is philosophical theology? How does philosophy relate to theology? Should theology be philosophical? This book explores answers to these questions from the ancient world to the present day, introducing the reader to the basic theories and thinkers in philosophical theology, within the Judaeo-Christian tradition. The book guides readers through the basic theories and thinkers in western philosophical theology from Plato to Plantinga, presenting key concerns that have led to debates within secular and Christian philosophy throughout history and encouraging readers to engage with these debates. It explores theories and schools of thought that have been developed to try and answer some of the most pressing questions in philosophy and theology across the following areas: faith and knowledge arguments for the existence of God mysticism religious language and experience the soul and life after death good and evil conscience and religious ethics human freewill divine providence and miracles Accessibly written, this book is an ideal starting point for anyone seeking a full introduction to philosophical theology as well as broader themes in philosophy of religion and systematic theology.

title: The Contemporary Relevance of Ratnatraya in Jain Philosophy: An Ethical and Epistemological Inquiry
abstract: Abstract: The Jain philosophy is one of the major philosophical traditions of Indian philosophical traditions. It is a deeply spiritual and ethical philosophy. The Jain thinkers do not believe in the existence of God or in the authority of the Vedic scriptures. Therefore, Jain philosophy is called nastika darsana. However, they believe in Moksha or liberation of the soul. The core ethical principle of Jainism is compassion and non-violence toward all living beings. In the contemporary world, marked by increasing violence and social discord, The Jain Tirthankaras advocate peace and harmony through the Ratnatraya – Samyak Darsana, Samyak jnana and Samyak charitra. Jain philosophy articulates that Ratnatraya constitutes the foundation of Jain ethics. Traditionally articulated in the Tattvartha Sutra as the necessary and sufficient conditions for moksha, this triad invites renewed philosophical scrutiny in light of 21st -century crises. This paper argues that beyond its eschatological function, the Ratnatraya offers a coherent apparatus for addressing ecological degradation, epistemic polarization, and ethical uncertainty. Samyak Darshana, grounded in the Jain ontology of jiva-ajiva and the principle of ahimsa, provides conceptual resources for non-anthropocentric environmental ethics. Samyak Jnana, articulated through Anekantavada and Syadvada, advances a model of epistemic pluralism and fallibilism pertinent to misinformation and ideological dogmatism in digital public spheres. Samyak Charitra, enacted through vows of restraint and aparigraha, proposes a paradigm of sustainable agency that critiques consumer capitalism and aligns with contemporary virtue ethics. While originating in monastic contexts, the Ratnatraya demonstrates adaptability for secular ethical and epistemological discourse. The paper concludes by considering limitations and future applications in education, policy, and interfaith dialogue.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Ist Existenz eine Eigenschaft? Und existiert also Gott? Eine Analyse von Existenzmodalitäten, Virtualität und Gödels Gottesbeweis.
abstract: Dieser Text untersucht die Frage, ob Existenz als Eigenschaft verstanden werden kann und welche Konsequenzen dies für metaphysische und logische Systeme hat. Ausgehend von klassischen Existenzmodalitäten (faktisch, möglich, unmöglich, notwendig) analysiert der Artikel die Rolle von Virtualität, Realität und Konstruktion in Wahrnehmung, Psychologie, Mathematik und Physik. Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der Frage, ob Existenz selbst eine Eigenschaft sein kann und ob aus dieser Annahme die Existenz Gottes folgt, wie es Gödel in seinem ontologischen Beweis formalisiert hat. Der Text diskutiert die Struktur von Eigenschaften, die Rolle von Virtualität und Realität, die Emergenz von Objekten und Begriffen sowie die Grenzen logischer Beweise im Bereich metaphysischer Entitäten. Der Artikel verbindet mathematische Logik, Ontologie, Semiotik, Physik und philosophische Anthropologie und bietet eine originäre Perspektive auf die Frage, was es bedeutet, zu existieren. This text examines whether existence can be understood as a property and what consequences this has for metaphysical and logical systems. Beginning with classical modalities of existence (factual, possible, impossible, necessary), the article analyzes the role of virtuality, reality, and construction in perception, psychology, mathematics, and physics. A central focus is the question of whether existence itself can be considered a property and whether this assumption implies the existence of God, as formalized in Gödel’s ontological proof. The text discusses the structure of properties, the interplay between virtuality and reality, the emergence of objects and concepts, and the limits of logical proofs concerning metaphysical entities. The article integrates mathematical logic, ontology, semiotics, physics, and philosophical anthropology, offering an original perspective on what it means to exist.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: ‘From Then on, to Feel Fear Was Normal for Us’ India (Punjab)
abstract: Prologue: Jagroop Singh Sherpur, 11 February 1991, Thulewal, Barnala Jagroop Singh Sherpur, a veterinary pharmacist and the state-level president of Punjab's Rationalist Society, was shot dead by Sikh separatist (Khalistani) militants at his hospital in Thulewal, south Punjab, on 11 February 1991.1 Well aware of the threat – ‘unidentified men, sometimes as many as ten, would circle our house’, recalls his son, Sukhraj, who was seven at the time – Jagroop had taken protective measures, purchasing a rifle and building a morcha (brick bunker) at the top of his house.2 However, as a Tarksheel sympathiser put it to me, ‘if you are on hospital duty a rifle cannot defend anyone’.3 Described by Megh Raj Mittar, a schoolteacher and one of the founders of Tarksheel, as a ‘fearless warrior ( nidhadak yodha ) … [who] was not scared of the terrorists’, Jagroop had reportedly ‘solved the [ghost and spirit possession] cases of hundreds of people [in the area] and entertained thousands [more] through magic tricks’ (performed in order to expose the mundane trickery behind the magic and miracles claimed by wandering sadhu s [ascetics] and godmen) (Mittar 1998: 108). Though loved by his fellow activists, they are quick to recall their frustration with Jagroop: ‘[W]e forbade him from entering into an open debate with the terrorists, [but] he ignored our instructions’ (Mittar 1998: 108). ‘He would wear his ideology on his sleeve.’ ‘He would speak his mind without paying any heed to the circumstances or conditions around him.’ ‘He didn't care whether someone was armed or not; he was too bold for the times.’4 Punjab's rationalists, even at the best of times, tend to shy away from publicly arguing against the existence of God or naysaying the inviolable sacredness of the Granth Sahib , the Sikh holy book.

title: Ist Existenz eine Eigenschaft? Und existiert also Gott? Eine Analyse von Existenzmodalitäten, Virtualität und Gödels Gottesbeweis.
abstract: Dieser Text untersucht die Frage, ob Existenz als Eigenschaft verstanden werden kann und welche Konsequenzen dies für metaphysische und logische Systeme hat. Ausgehend von klassischen Existenzmodalitäten (faktisch, möglich, unmöglich, notwendig) analysiert der Artikel die Rolle von Virtualität, Realität und Konstruktion in Wahrnehmung, Psychologie, Mathematik und Physik. Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der Frage, ob Existenz selbst eine Eigenschaft sein kann und ob aus dieser Annahme die Existenz Gottes folgt, wie es Gödel in seinem ontologischen Beweis formalisiert hat. Der Text diskutiert die Struktur von Eigenschaften, die Rolle von Virtualität und Realität, die Emergenz von Objekten und Begriffen sowie die Grenzen logischer Beweise im Bereich metaphysischer Entitäten. Der Artikel verbindet mathematische Logik, Ontologie, Semiotik, Physik und philosophische Anthropologie und bietet eine originäre Perspektive auf die Frage, was es bedeutet, zu existieren. This text examines whether existence can be understood as a property and what consequences this has for metaphysical and logical systems. Beginning with classical modalities of existence (factual, possible, impossible, necessary), the article analyzes the role of virtuality, reality, and construction in perception, psychology, mathematics, and physics. A central focus is the question of whether existence itself can be considered a property and whether this assumption implies the existence of God, as formalized in Gödel’s ontological proof. The text discusses the structure of properties, the interplay between virtuality and reality, the emergence of objects and concepts, and the limits of logical proofs concerning metaphysical entities. The article integrates mathematical logic, ontology, semiotics, physics, and philosophical anthropology, offering an original perspective on what it means to exist.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Cogito Ergo Sum and Tat Tvam Asi: Parallels between René Descartes and Adi Shankaracharya
abstract: The paper undertakes a comparative philosophical study of the thought of René Descartes and Adi Shankaracharya, centring on the thematic convergence between the Cartesian dictum "Cogito, ergo sum" and the Vedāntic mahāvākya "Tat Tvam Asi", "Aham Brahmasmi", etc. Beginning with Descartes' method of methodological scepticism as articulated in Meditations on First Philosophy, the study highlights how radical doubt functions as an epistemological tool to arrive at indubitable certainty, culminating in the affirmation of the thinking self.This is placed in dialogue with the Upanishadic method of neti, neti, which similarly negates empirical reality but extends beyond epistemology into ontological realization.The paper further examines Descartes' conception of the self as res cogitans in relation to the Vedāntic understanding of Ātman as pure, self-revealing consciousness, arguing that while Descartes establishes certainty at the level of reflective thought, Advaita Vedānta transcends thought itself to assert non-dual awareness.The study also compares Descartes' rational proofs for the existence of God with Indian approaches to ultimate reality, noting parallels with the Upanishadic conception of Brahman as infinite and self-evident, while emphasizing the Vedāntic shift from logical demonstration to direct experiential realization (aparokṣānubhūti).In addressing mind-body interaction, Descartes' pineal gland hypothesis is contrasted with the Indian model of antaḥkaraṇa, which offers a more elaborate psychological framework integrating cognition, memory, and ego, and further situates the mind within the broader pursuit of liberation (mokṣa).Additionally, Descartes' mechanistic view of nature is examined alongside the Sāṅkhya theory of prakṛti and the doctrine of the three guṇas, demonstrating how Indian philosophy accommodates both causal regularity and qualitative diversity, enriched by the metaphysical concept of māyā.The paper argues title: Ajattelu mielipiteitä jakavissa aiheissa : Ontologisen, episteemisen ja motivoituneen kognition rooli
abstract: This dissertation consists of three studies that set out to explain people’s reasoning on polarizing issues. Two vastly differing types of thinking were examined. First, how people perceive the relationship between science and religion: as being in conflict, in dialogue, separate, or possible to integrate. The second type of thinking concerned how people perceive the quality of arguments providing justifications either for or against currently contested, i.e., hot, topics. The arguments included either questionable or more solid justifications for a claim. An example of a poorly justified argument is to state that “Euthanasia should not be allowed because it will allow killing people simply because they are an inconvenience to someone”. While there are no correct answers to the question of how science and religion relate to each other, perceptions of argument quality can be considered more or less accurate. Across the various polarizing issues, the results demonstrated motivated cognition, as individuals’ personal attitudes toward the topic(s) at hand clearly influenced their perceptions. In addition, individuals’ ontological cognition, especially the strength of their belief in the existence of God, played a large role in the way the science–religion relationship was perceived. Most notably, those viewing conflict and favoring science had the lowest belief in God and the least positive view of religion’s impact on society. In the evaluation of everyday arguments, the role of motivated cognition was seen in people favoring arguments that supported their attitudes. These findings suggest that people are biased by their personal attitudes and beliefs when they think about various types of issues. Finding ways to support people in being objective and tolerant appears thus important if we wish to lessen division and improve reasoning. Some potential ways of decreasing bias and thinking mistakes were found. The findings showed that acknowledging the human tendency to be biased by one’s subjective preferences and asking for objectivity led to slightly more objective and accurate argument evaluations compared to instructions that turned attention to people’s personal values and convictions. These findings urge us to pay attention to how discussions are set up. The results also indicated that people’s epistemic cognition, i.e., their views about knowledge and their tendencies to think analytically, shape how people think about polarizing issues. Some evidence was attained that people with less advanced epistemic cognition are more likely to show biased and closed-minded thinking. However, this was most clearly the case when one view could be considered more accurate than another, particularly regarding improved detection of problems in poorly justified arguments irrespective of individuals’ attitudes. There is thus more hope for epistemic cognition to increase accuracy than impartiality. Still, these findings encourage the teaching of critical thinking skills, including science literacy, and the creation of environments that support reflective reasoning in order to improve everyday thinking.

title: χ‑Absolute and the God of World Religions: Structural Isomorphism Between Scientific and Theological Concepts of the Absolute
abstract: Abstract This article develops a fully formalized operator–spectral analysis of the structural isomorphism between the χ‑Absolute—the fundamental zero‑structure of reality in the ZEBTS‑SUPER 12.0 framework—and the concept of the Absolute (God) in the major monotheistic traditions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. χ‑Absolute is defined by the universal operator equation Aχ ψ = 0, representing a non‑spatial, non‑temporal, self‑sufficient, zero‑entropy ontological ground. This zero‑structure is embedded within the canonical χ‑ontological chain Aχ → ζχ → Sχ → κχ → π₁(Mχ) → Kχ < 0, which deterministically generates spectral density, boundary stress, geometric curvature, topological connectivity, and hyperbolic geometry. Each level of the chain is governed by χ‑Trinity identities ensuring structural balance and ontological consistency. The article demonstrates that χ‑Absolute possesses the same ontological attributes traditionally ascribed to the theological Absolute: unity, simplicity, transcendence, non‑temporality, non‑spatiality, self‑sufficiency, and epistemic inaccessibility. In Judaism, Ein Sof is described as infinite, undifferentiated, and unknowable; in Christianity, the apophatic God is pure actuality (Actus Purus) and manifests through Logos; in Islam, Tawhid affirms absolute unity, while Baqa affirms eternal invariance. These attributes correspond precisely to the operator–spectral properties of χ‑Absolute. The mechanism of χ‑projections—structured manifestations of χ‑Absolute through the χ‑chain—is shown to be structurally equivalent to theological models of creation. The emergence of spectral density (ζχ), boundary constraints (Sχ), curvature (κχ), topology (π₁(Mχ)), and hyperbolic geometry (Kχ < 0) corresponds to the emanation of sefirot from Ein Sof, the creative activity of Logos, and the contingent creation through divine will (irada). χ‑collapse, the operator–spectral selection of admissible χ‑projections, is structurally analogous to theological volition, though non‑personal and non‑intentional. ZEBTS‑SUPER experiments at energies ~10⁻³³ eV detect χ‑noise, χ‑fluctuations, χ‑residues, χ‑boundary transitions, and χ‑spectral gaps—phenomenological traces of χ‑Absolute. These traces correspond structurally to Shekhinah (Judaism), divine energies (Christianity), and the 99 Names of Allah (Islam). Thus χ‑phenomenology constitutes the scientific analog of divine manifestation. The article also demonstrates that χ‑Trinity identities—such as Ord(0) + Ord(1) + Ord(∞) = 0, κχ + Sχ + λ₀ = 0, and Kχ + κχ + λ₀ = 0—are structurally analogous to theological triadic models: the Christian Trinity, Kabbalistic triads, and Islamic metaphysical triads. These identities express unity of essence, multiplicity of modes, and structural balance. Despite profound structural isomorphism, χ‑Absolute diverges from the theological Absolute in three essential domains: personality, will, and moral agency. χ‑Absolute is non‑personal, non‑volitional, and non‑moral, whereas the God of monotheism is personal, intentional, and ethically normative. Thus χ‑Absolute is structurally identical to the metaphysical Absolute, but not to the personal God of religious practice. The article concludes that χ‑Absolute does not constitute evidence for the existence of God. Instead, it provides the first scientifically formalized operator–spectral reconstruction of the metaphysical Absolute, establishing a new conceptual bridge between physics and theology. This bridge enables the emergence of χ‑Theology, operator–spectral metaphysics, apophatic physics, and a unified ontological framework integrating scientific and theological conceptions of the Absolute.

title: Размышления Ф. М. Достоевского о проблемах страдания, гордости и бунта против Бога в романе «Идиот»
abstract: Объектом исследования является роман Ф. М. Достоевского «Идиот», а предметом – художественное воплощение проблем страдания, гордости и бунта против Бога в образах Ипполита Терентьева и князя Мышкина, а также размышления Ф. М. Достоевского о страдании. В статье анализируются монологи, сны и самоубийство Ипполита, раскрываются причины его сомнений в Боге и в законах природы, а также его бунт против религиозной логики достижения искупления через страдания: самоубийство Ипполита было одновременно личной трагедией и крайним актом борьбы против веры в Бога. Князь Мышкин, напротив, воплощает христианское смирение и сострадание, рассматривая страдание как путь к спасению души. Сопоставление этих двух образов отражает основную идею Ф. М. Достоевского: страдание может быть как путем спасения в вере, так и вести к разрушительному протесту. Методология исследования в данной статье основана на анализе текста романа Ф. М. Достоевского «Идиот» с широким использованием соответствующих научных работ (академических статей, монографий и критических статей), посвященных Ипполиту и князю Мышкину. Новизна исследования заключается в том, что в статье раскрывается новое видение Ф. М. Достоевского о проблеме человеческого страдания. Смирение князя Мышкина воплощает традиционное религиозное представление об искуплении через страдание, однако самоубийство Ипполита указывает на другой исход: страдание может породить сомнения, которые перерастут в бунт, что в конечном итоге приведет к гибели личности. Основные выводы заключаются в том, что Ипполит признавал существование Бога, но не мог принять созданный Им мировой порядок, наполненный страданиями. Его самоубийство было вызвано не атеизмом, а гордым бунтом – крайним протестом против христианской логики, согласно которой искупление достигается через страдания. Через зеркальное противопоставление князю Мышкину, олицетворяющему смирение и искупление, в статье раскрывается двойственность страдания в мысли Ф. М. Достоевского: страдание является одновременно путем к религиозному спасению и эстетическим явлением, способным даровать духовную силу и возвысить характер. В конечном итоге трагическая судьба Ипполита проявляет вечную диалектику между верой и сомнением, покорностью и бунтом, становится воплощением размышлений Ф. М. Достоевского о существовании человечества. The object of the study is F. M. Dostoevsky’s novel “The Idiot”, and the subject is the artistic embodiment of the problems of suffering, pride and rebellion against God in the images of Hippolytus Terentyev and Prince Myshkin, as well as F. M. Dostoevsky’s reflections on suffering. The work analyzes Hippolytus’s soliloquies, dreams, and suicide to reveal his skepticism toward God and natural laws, as well as his rebellion against the religious logic of “redemption through suffering”. Hippolytus’s suicide represents both a personal tragedy and defiance of faith in God; in contrast, Prince Myshkin embodies Christian humility and compassion, viewing suffering as a path to redemption. This contrast embodies Dostoevsky’s central thesis: suffering can lead to redemptive faith or ignite destructive rebellion. The research methodology is based on an analysis of the novel by F. M. Dostoevsky “The Idiot” with the widespread application of relevant scientific works (research papers, monographs and critical articles) focusing on Hippolytus and Prince Myshkin. The article also reveals a new vision of F. M. Dostoevsky about the issue of human suffering. Prince Myshkin’s humility embodies the traditional religious notion of redemption through suffering, however Hippolytus’s suicide points to a different outcome: suffering can give rise to doubts that escalate into rebellion, leading to the death of the personality. The paper concludes that Hippolytus recognized the existence of God, but could not accept the world order created by Him, filled with suffering. His suicide springs from a proud protest, not atheistic denial. Through his mirrored contrast with Myshkin, Dostoevsky reveals suffering’s dual nature – both a path to religious redemption and an opportunity for spiritual elevation. Thus the tragic fate of Hippolytus shows an eternal dialectic between faith and doubt, humility and rebellion, becomes the embodiment of F. M. Dostoevsky’s thoughts about the existence of humanity.

title: Fate in Ancient Greek Philosophy and Religion
abstract: The Greek term heimarmene, rendered in Latin as fatum and in English as “fate” (and occasionally as “destiny”), designates a doctrinal notion situated at the intersection of Greek religion and philosophy. The analysis of the interplay between the purported causality of fate and that of other forms of causation is a complex undertaking, closely connected with a range of religious questions. Reflection on fate gives rise to fundamental philosophical issues, including those concerning contingent futures, freedom of the will, determinism, divine foreknowledge, and providence. Furthermore, this theme is intertwined with numerous human situations prominently depicted in Greek epic and tragic literature—indeed, it has exercised a lasting influence on Western literature as a whole. Such situations include unexpected good fortune, the mortal inability to withstand misfortune, the practice of divination, and the relationship between human beings and the divine. Given the enduring relevance of themes such as free will, determinism, and divine foreknowledge within contemporary philosophy of religion, it is particularly fruitful to investigate how these questions were addressed not only by Greek philosophers but also by other Greek authors who are not typically classified as philosophers. In late antiquity, Greek thought revisited the problem of fate and divine providence within the framework of Christian theology, engaging in close dialogue with so-called “pagan” philosophical traditions. These exchanges constitute a significant contribution to the metaphysical understanding of fate.

title: THE NATURE OF TIME: Trialogue of Science Philosophy and Religion Vision of Time
abstract: The phenomenon of time remains one of the most foundational, recalcitrant, and under-determined categories of human inquiry. While the natural sciences successfully formalize and measure the operational properties of time, they lack a universally accepted ontological definition of what time is at the bedrock of Being. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. Part I (Science) identifies the precise junctures at which modern theoretical physics — particularly the problem of time in quantum gravity, the cosmological singularity, and the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems — reaches the outer boundary of empirical formalisms.Part II (Philosophy) constructs an autonomous metaphysical architecture upon this threshold: a three-tiered taxonomy of temporality (causal TIME-1, cyclical Time-2, and evental/phenomenal time-3). From this foundation the work develops a periodic scale of temporal densities, an ontology of organic lifespan governed by discrete chronon allocations, a ninefold intentional matrix of temporal perception, and an account of civilizational and spiritual impetus.Part III (Religion) establishes a sustained conceptual dialogue with the Abrahamic traditions and formulates the structural paradigm of the “ascending spiral” as a rigorous alternative to the exhausted dichotomy between linear-historical and cyclical-cosmological temporalities. The original contribution of the dissertation does not consist in a claim to resolve open technical problems of theoretical physics — a pretension the work explicitly rejects. Its novelty resides in the overarching architecture of the synthesis: the three-tiered taxonomy as an epistemological instrument capable of sustaining physics, phenomenology, and theology in coherent relation without domain conflation, and the model of the ascending spiral as a conceptual bridge reconciling eternity, cosmic periodicity, and teleological becoming. The final chapters integrate this architecture within the author’s paradigm of Informational Monism.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
