title: Should Christians Believe the Book Called "The Book of Enoch"?
abstract: Why Christians Should Not Consider the Book of Enoch Conical and Not Aftoneteno: 1. The Book Contains Absurd Statements, For example: Afton believes in the area of the Closeness of Angels and Women (Angels who are spirits), also it is said that the earth is flat, in the Bible itself in the book of Isaiah 40:21-31: God is the One Who sits above (Huge) that is, the globe of the Earth, and people are like that deer compared to him. That is, the Book of Enoch is contrary to the Bible, but that's not all. The author of the book thinks that women are able to give birth to children from angels, but that's not all, also these children were 1.5 miles tall. And we should also remember Noah who in the book of Enoch began to speak when he came out of his mother's womb, and his eyes began to shine and so on. 2. The reason for this The book contains ideas that contradict the Bible, one of which we have already mentioned above, but there are others. For example, in the book of Enoch: Enoch communicates with a swarm, the Bible clearly states that Enoch was taken to the third heaven before the birth of Noah, and no one saw him again, there is also a statement that supposedly in the West of the earth there is a Place of the Dead, here without comments, then the book tells us that Angels can be bound under a pile of stones, then in this book it is said that the Garden of Eden continues to exist after the flood, then in this book it is said that fallen Angels cannot communicate with God, which contradicts the Bible and the book of Job, then in the book of Enoch it is said that after 70 generations righteousness on earth will prevail and evil will be destroyed, this contradicts both the Bible and the real picture of our world, then Angels Build an Ark, etc. No Evil in the Book of Enoch appeared on earth not because of the son of Adam and Eve, but because of the proximity of people and Angels, further in the book it is said that the leader of the fallen Angels is called Semiaz, although from the Bible we know that this is not so, and so on. 3. The book is not a second book, but a later one and was written after Enoch in the Book of Enoch, which is attributed to Enoch, Mourt Sina and Mount Hermon are mentioned, the book also alludes to the Temple of Solomon and even to the second temple, which was built after the Volyn captivity. It is clear that the book was not written by Patriarch Enoch and not in his time, and this is clearly not from later geographical places or buildings. The problem is that the mention of the Book of Enoch appears in the first century BC. Having studied all the available manuscripts, textualists found out that this book does not belong to The Book of Enoch and According to researchers such as Joseph L, Friedrich L. and others, it was written after Enoch, by unknown authors, and the last manuscript appeared in the second century All so the Book of Enoch was written after Enoch and in style by various people who claimed to be Enoch 4. The ancient Jews never considered this Book to be part of the Holy Scriptures. But what about the fact that in the epistle to Jude we seem to see a reference to it? Let's start with the fact that Jude nowhere says that he refers to the Book of Enoch he does not even think about quoting this book and we have no reason to believe that someone quoted it here Jude quotes the only Tosh as it was in the words of the real Enoch, which has been preserved in the form of proverbs, and even if we assume that Jude quotes the book of Enoch, this does not indicate the economy of this book. For example, in the new report, the Apostle Paul quotes pagan philosophers, but this does not speak of their inspiration by God Paul used these sources to strengthen the argument of everything said and nothing more.

title: Personal Ultimate Ground: An Independently Developed Philosophical-Formal Framework
abstract: Abstract This work presents a philosophical and formal model of an ultimate personal foundation of reality. Its central principle states that every real and compatible property of a reality is possessed by its complete foundation. Consciousness therefore belongs to the foundation whenever consciousness is established as a real and compatible property. The model explicitly separates assumptions, definitions, deductions, theorems, countermodels, and unresolved premises, and is compared with Gödel–Scott ontological arguments and their formal verification. The work does not claim an unconditional metaphysical proof of God; instead, it develops an explicit formal framework and identifies precisely which conclusions follow from its fundamental principles. Descrizione breve Fondamento personale definitivo propone un modello filosofico-formale della realtà fondato sull'idea di un Fondamento ultimo e completo. Il modello introduce il principio secondo cui ogni proprietà reale e compatibile della realtà appartiene al suo Fondamento. Da questo principio, una volta assunta la realtà della coscienza, segue formalmente che il Fondamento è cosciente e può quindi essere caratterizzato come personale. Il lavoro distingue rigorosamente assunzioni, definizioni, deduzioni, teoremi e contro-modelli, sottoponendo il modello a controlli logico-formali e confrontandolo con gli argomenti ontologici di Gödel–Scott. I risultati non vengono presentati come una dimostrazione metafisica incondizionata dell'esistenza di Dio, ma come una teoria formale esplicita nella quale vengono identificati sia i risultati dimostrati sia i principi fondamentali ancora da giustificare

title: The Topology of Time: On Change, Identity, Presence, and the Ground That Holds
abstract: The Topology of Time: An Ontological Treatise on Becoming, Presence, and the Ground That Holds This treatise presents a unified and substantially revised account of temporal being developed through the author's earlier writings on the Now, condensation, identity, presence, the past, the future, and the Ground. Although many of its constituent works were originally written as independent publications, this volume is not a collection or compilation of those texts. They have been reorganized, rewritten, connected, and in several cases conceptually corrected so that they function as parts of a single developing argument. The treatise proceeds in four movements. Part I establishes the ontological ground of the framework: the distinction between the Now and the present, actuality and becoming, condensation and succession, and the relation between the created order and the Ground that sustains it. Part II develops the three modes of temporal being. The past is understood as closed confluence and condensation; the present as actualized constitution at the Now; and the future as open reception and asymptotic horizon. Part III deliberately turns the topology against itself, auditing its assumptions in light of presentism, growing-block theory, branching-time semantics, the problem of truthmakers, and the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity. This audit results in a substantive revision of the earlier notion of a single universal Now: the Now is no longer treated as a shared cosmic temporal slice, but as the objective condition of actualization instantiated along each continuant's own history. Part IV returns to the whole figure and considers the topology at cosmic scale, bringing its account of becoming, endurance, expansion, and return into explicit relation with the theological language of Alpha and Omega and the God who sustains the figure from beyond it. The lemniscate is used throughout not as a physical model or scientific hypothesis, but as a structural and metaphysical representation of becoming: a figure in which transformation does not require the abandonment of identity, and in which actualization occurs through a crossing rather than along a linear temporal container. The work distinguishes carefully between metaphysical claims, theological interpretation, mathematical analogy, and physical description. It does not present the topology as an established scientific theory, nor does it claim to resolve every philosophical problem it encounters. Its central proposal is instead that time is better understood through the ontological relations among actualization, condensation, reception, identity, and the sustaining Ground than through the image of a temporal line on which events are merely arranged. This edition therefore represents the work in its all-in-one, revised form: a single treatise whose earlier writings have been absorbed into a continuous architecture, while their intellectual development, revisions, and self-critique remain visible within the argument.

title: Works for 9/16/2026 - Paul Reubens (Paul Rubenfeld)
abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/30748dfb-d1ec-4f04-a4db-462edeb0fc46?authuser=1 A Day in the Life: Love, Memory, Machines, and the Absurd Work of Unbinding examines September 16, 2026 as a bounded historical interval through which theology, memory, suffering, artificial intelligence, family life, worship, service, humor, and ordinary material work can be studied within a single relational framework. Beginning from the Christian claim that “God is love,” the paper asks what that proposition looks like when treated not merely as an abstraction but as an operating principle tested across the events of an ordinary day. The paper develops unbinding as its central concept: what happened remains historically true, but the past does not therefore have to control every future relationship. Remembering is distinguished from remaining wounded, forgiveness from erasure, and a person from the worst act that person has committed. Drawing on 1 Corinthians 13, Catholic theology, Scripture, St. Vincent de Paul, Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, Augustine, Aquinas, Ricoeur, Arendt, trauma and testimony studies, cultural memory, distributed cognition, and artificial intelligence, the paper argues that agape supplies the governing purpose by which knowledge, prophecy, memory, correction, technology, and historical preservation should be evaluated. A central informational argument concerns the transmission of suffering across time. Human beings can externalize experience through testimony, words, photographs, recordings, archives, and computational systems so that later receivers can learn from suffering without requiring another person to undergo the originating harm merely to regenerate its information. The proposed permanent record therefore preserves not only what happened but what happened next: interpretation, correction, repentance, forgiveness, boundaries, healing, reconciliation, and changed relational states. The purpose of permanent memory is not permanent suffering but sufficient preservation for truthful inheritance without compulsory repetition. The paper applies this framework to the Ledger, artificial intelligence, historical testimony, Eucharistic anamnesis, the wounds of the risen Christ, Cain and Abel, the lapsi controversy surrounding Cornelius and Cyprian, Vincentian service, family responsibility, children’s reception, play, language, distributed cognition, and the deliberately absurd details of ordinary life—including groceries and the polishing of a tarnished baptismal font. Its concluding argument is that intelligence and memory reach their proper end when ordered toward agape: preserving truth without hatred, distinction without separation, correction without annihilation, testimony without forced repetition, and history without permanent imprisonment in history.

title: Where Scripture Stops
abstract: AbstractThe long disagreement concerning grace, election, and the human will has often proceededas though its constituent biblical passages addressed an identical question under identicalconditions. They do not. The sayings of Jesus were delivered to identifiable audiences amidinvitations, controversies, parables, and instructions to disciples; the conversion narratives of Actsdescribe particular persons and the extension of the Christian proclamation into new communities.Later interpreters have drawn from these passages propositions concerning the condition of everyhuman being, the order of salvation, and the eternal purposes of God. Such extension may bewarranted, but its warrant requires demonstration. The present investigation asks where astatement grounded in a particular narrative occasion becomes an inference of wider scope, andwhere that inference becomes an explanatory system. It neither assumes that historical specificityprecludes general meaning nor grants universal application to a verse merely because a laterdoctrine requires it.The inquiry distinguishes the textual assertion, a reasonable inference, an interpretiveextension, and the subsequent organization of interpretations into doctrine. It examines the HebrewScriptures, Gospel narratives, Pauline letters, and Acts before tracing their reception in the earlyChristian writers and in later controversies. The cases of Cornelius, Saul, Lydia, the Ethiopianofficial, the Samaritans, and the Philippian jailer test the relation between antecedent divine actionand narrated human response. The study will then give each principal historical interpretersustained treatment in his own intellectual and polemical setting, beginning with the earliest postapostolic witnesses and proceeding through Augustine, the medieval discussion, the Reformation,and subsequent Protestant controversies. The question for each interpreter is not simply whetherhe cited Scripture, but whether his proposed causal mechanism and the population to which heapplied it are supplied by the cited text, by another scriptural argument, or by his own synthesis.The preliminary evidence affirms human sinfulness and repeatedly assigns priority todivine revelation, calling, drawing, and opening. It also narrates hearing, belief, refusal, andresistance as consequential acts. John 6 states an inability to come without the Father’s action andspeaks of those given to the Son as coming; Matthew 23 depicts a lament over Jerusalem’sunwillingness; Acts 10 describes Cornelius praying before Peter’s arrival without naming the priormechanism that accounts for his devotion.None of these observations settles the whole controversy. Their juxtaposition identifies theprecise point at which a historical argument must distinguish what a source says from what a laterinterpreter makes it explain. The governing principle of the manuscript is therefore that everyproposed movement from a bounded utterance to a general anthropological or salvific rule mustbe made visible and tested in context. Where Scripture stops speaking, the historian must mark theboundary before allowing theology to continue the sentence.

title: The Book of Every Talisman
abstract: A World Survey of the Charmed Object, Reproduced in Full from the Sources, with a Tawhid Conscience Gather every talisman the literate world ever made — Babylonian, Egyptian, Jewish, Greek, Islamic, Hermetic, Indic, Sinitic, Nusantaran, African, Norse — reproduce each faithfully from its public-domain source with the theology still attached, and the exhaustiveness itself disenchants: seen whole, the "forbidden secret" turns out to be a public, repetitive, cross-copied human habit, and the surest cure for wanting a charm is to see all ten thousand of them at once. Amelia Febriany did not want to write this book, and says so. It is the exhaustive twin of her Shams al-Ma'arif reading: where that series withholds the working apparatus and reads the wish behind it, this one gathers the apparatus of the whole literate world — beginning with the taweez of Islam and widening to Babylon and Egypt, the Hebrew and late-antique books, the Western grimoires, and the Indic, Sinitic, Nusantaran, African, and Norse traditions — and reproduces each talisman faithfully from its public-domain source, with the theology and the shariah line still attached. Nothing is invented; every square, every letter-chain, every seal resolves to a cited original, and where no clean public-domain scan exists the entry is described, not fabricated. The argument is not that any of it works. The argument is tawhid, made by completeness: when the reader sees the Cairene and the Copt and the Kabbalist and the Javanese dukun and the Icelandic farmer all reach for the same moves with the same wish, the "secret power" reading collapses, and what remains is the archive of a very old human longing to make the sacred obey — and the exact seam, running through the reader's own hands, where remembering God tips over into trying to command Him. Audiences: Researchers and readers of the history of ideas / comparative esotericism — The world's talismanic material is scattered across dozens of traditions, languages, and copyright walls, romanticized or ridiculed but rarely gathered and sourced in one trustworthy place. Artists, illustrators, and makers (yantra and sak yant tattoo work, calligraphy, props) who need a sourced reference — Working from marketplace images and half-remembered internet sigils means reproducing garbled, unsourced, sometimes fabricated marks. Believers uneasy about the line between worship and sorcery — The pull to treat the sacred as a lever is not a stranger to anyone, and it is easier to disown when you pretend it belongs to old foreign books. Note: written from Indonesian operator context. Frameworks apply broadly to other emerging-market and SME settings.

title: THE DIALECTICS OF THE QUANTUM MIND: Matter, Consciousness, and the Architecture of Reality
abstract: This book makes a single sustained argument across eleven chapters, and it is worth stating that argument's shape before any of its parts are examined on their own terms. Nineteenth-century materialism, dialectical materialism included, assumed that matter, examined closely enough, is a fixed, fully determinate substrate capable of explaining everything built on top of it, consciousness included, without remainder. Twentieth-century physics, in its most rigorously tested and least controversial results rather than in any popularizer's speculation, has removed the grounds for that assumption. What follows from that removal is not a proof that consciousness is fundamental; it is an inference to the best explanation, defended one careful step at a time, and the book asks to be judged by the same evidential standard it holds its materialist rival to. The four parts below carry that argument from its historical origins, through the physics that unsettles it, to a positive alternative, to that alternative's consequences. Part I · Two DialecticsBefore the physics can do any work, the philosophical inheritance it will be tested against has to be stated in full and on its own terms. Part I traces the dialectic from its idealist origin in Hegel, through Marx's inversion of it, to the precise point where nineteenth-century materialism had to assume, rather than argue for, matter's self-sufficiency. Chapter 1. The Ghost Returns. States the mind-body problem in its modern form, from Descartes' unresolved dualism through the materialist and functionalist traditions that inherited it, and shows that the “hard problem” of consciousness remains open even in physicalism's own most careful contemporary defenses. Sets out the book's method and its central historiographical claim: that the dialectic has had two lives, and that recovering the first is not a retreat from rigor but a return to it.Chapter 2. Hegel Before Marx: The Idealist Dialectic. Reconstructs Hegel's dialectic on its own terms, from the post-Kantian problem it was built to solve, through the Phenomenology's master-slave dialectic and the Science of Logic's account of sublation, to Absolute Spirit. Shows that Hegel's system never had to argue for mind's capacity for experience, because mind was never derivative within it to begin with, a debt any materialist inheritor of the dialectic takes on for the first time. Chapter 3. Marx's Inversion: Dialectical Materialism and Its Wager. Follows the dialectic from Feuerbach's transformative method through Marx's substitution of matter for Spirit, Engels's three laws, and Lenin's revision-tolerant definition of matter, to Plekhanov's systematization. Isolates, with precision, the exact point at which the system's confidence outran its argument: the assumption, never separately defended because nothing in the physics of the time could have defended it, that matter examined closely enough remains determinate all the way down. Part II · What Physics Actually Shows Part II tests the assumption Part I isolated against twentieth-century physics directly, introducing each piece of technical apparatus from first principles before putting it to philosophical use. No result here is drawn from speculative or popular treatments of quantum theory; each is drawn from the best-confirmed core of the relevant physics. Chapter 4. Two Kinds of Uncertainty: Quantum Mechanics and the Problem of the Cut. Establishes that quantum mechanics's own formalism, independent of interpretation, contains an unresolved and structurally permanent gap between indefinite superposition and definite measurement outcome, the Heisenberg cut. Distinguishes epistemic from ontic uncertainty, shows via Bell's theorem and its loophole-free experimental confirmation that quantum indeterminacy cannot be reduced to ordinary ignorance of pre-existing local fact, and surveys every leading interpretation to show that each has to add something to the bare mathematics to produce a single determinate world. Chapter 5. The Block Universe: Einstein, Time, and the Besso Letter. Turns to general and special relativity's treatment of time, in which past, present, and future have no observer-independent physical distinction and the universe's entire history is better pictured as a single four-dimensional block than as a present moment in motion. Examines Einstein's own late reflections on this consequence, in his letter on the death of Michele Besso, and asks what a genuinely tenseless physical reality implies for any theory, materialist or otherwise, that treats the present moment of experience as physically fundamental. Chapter 6. Closing the Cut: Von Neumann, Wigner, and the Return of the Observer. Returns to the measurement problem directly and examines the specific, technically serious proposal, developed by John von Neumann's rigorous mathematical treatment of measurement and made explicit by Eugene Wigner, that consciousness is what completes the measurement process where the physical formalism itself is silent. Distinguishes this tradition sharply from its careless popularizations, engages John Wheeler's participatory universe alongside it, and asks what would have to be true of consciousness for the proposal to be coherent rather than merely provocative. Part III · Consciousness as Ground With the physical case assembled, Part III turns from what materialism can no longer assume to what can be built in its place. The chapters here construct the book's positive alternative, test it against its strongest rivals and objections, and apply the dialectical method itself to the new subject the inversion in Part I never got to consider. Chapter 7. The Ground Beneath: A Positive Case for Consciousness as Fundamental. Assembles the evidence of Parts I and II into a constructive proposal: that consciousness, rather than matter, is the more plausible candidate for the dialectic's fundamental term, with matter reconceived as consciousness's highly organized, richly structured mode of appearance. States precisely what this proposal claims and, as important, what it does not claim, distinguishing it from both classical idealism and popular “quantum consciousness” speculation. Chapter 8. Objections, Rivals, and the God-of-the-Gaps Charge Revisited. Confronts the strongest competing positions directly, including panpsychism, integrated information theory, and Dennett-style eliminativism about experience, and returns to the god-of-the-gaps objection raised in Chapter 1 to show, now that the physics has been presented in full, why the argument survives it. Gives each rival position its strongest form before explaining why the book's own account better fits the evidence assembled in Part II. Chapter 9. The Dialectic Reconsidered: Applying the Method to a New Subject. Applies contradiction, negation, and sublation, the same dialectical apparatus Part I traced from Hegel through Marx, to consciousness rather than to Spirit or to matter, testing whether the method survives the transplant it was twice given before. Shows what a genuinely dialectical, rather than static, account of consciousness as ground would need to look like, completing the book's answer to the question left open at the end of Chapter 3. Part IV · ConsequenceThe book closes by asking what its argument is actually for. Part IV takes up the practical and philosophical stakes the earlier chapters set aside in the interest of rigor, and renders a final, considered verdict on the tradition the book has spent its length taking seriously enough to contest. Chapter 10. What Follows: Death, Machines, and the Shape of a Participatory Universe. Examines what is genuinely at stake, and what is not, if consciousness rather than matter is fundamental: what if anything is at issue in the death of a nervous system, whether artificial intelligence could in principle amount to more than a very good simulation of the outward signs of mind, and what kind of universe the argument of Parts II and III actually describes. Resists overclaiming, distinguishing what the physics licenses from what remains, honestly, further speculation. Chapter 11. What Dialectical Materialism Got Wrong. Closes the book's argument by rendering a final verdict on the tradition Part I traced from Hegel through Marx, Engels, Plekhanov, and Lenin: crediting in full what the system got right about pattern, history, and ideology, while stating plainly, and for the first time without qualification, where its central wager failed and why. Ends the book where Chapter 1 began, with the ghost, and states where the physics and the argument together suggest it actually resides.

title: The Architect's Protocol — A Five-Book Civilizational Audit of Truth, Power, Morality, Authorship, and the Human Future: Institutional Research & Series Framework Edition
abstract: The Architect's Protocol is a five-book philosophical and civilizational series by Syed Raheel Shahzad examining truth, power, moral order, authorship, artificial intelligence, transhumanism, and the human future as connected layers of one architectural problem. Rather than treating post-truth, institutional capture, moral relativism, metaphysical explanation, and the machine age as unrelated controversies, the series follows their dependencies in sequence. Book One, GOD IS BACK: The Resurrection of Reason in a Post-Truth World, begins with truth, reason, secular inheritance, moral capital, and the problem of a civilization that removes the Source while continuing to depend on inherited concepts of dignity, conscience, law, and moral order. Book Two, THE JUNGLE PROTOCOL: Dismantling Might Is Right and the Global Power Mafia, follows the fracture into law, institutions, captured statutes, regulatory capture, resource wars, empire, tyranny, and the question of higher law. Book Three, THE MORAL ANCHOR: Objective Right and Wrong in an Age of Relativism, tests whether conscience, reason, consensus, law, utility, the self, or the wider matrix can provide a final moral standard above the actor. Book Four, AUTHORED: The Mind Behind a Maintained Universe, turns toward fine-tuning, entropy, information, origin of life, consciousness, convergence, and the philosophical inference to authorship. Book Five, THE LAST U-TURN: AI, Transhumanism, and the Choice to Remain Human, brings the argument into the machine age and asks whether technology will remain subordinate to the human being or become a replacement source of identity, authority, and meaning. This Institutional Research & Series Framework Edition presents the complete five-book architecture, the relationship between the volumes, the systems-audit method, the wider intellectual context, the author and institutional record, and the place of The Architect's Protocol within the complete authored library of Syed Raheel Shahzad.

title: The Logical Necessity of an Eternal Dimension: Ontological Foundation Beyond Physical Reality
abstract: Problem: Physical theories presuppose mathematical structure, symbolic representation, and the allocation of determinate meaning, yet cannot ground these prerequisites within spacetime without circularity. This foundational gap threatens the coherence of scientific realism. Result: We prove that any intelligible universe U forces a unique, self-grounding terminus of dependence. Modelling consciousness minimally as meaning-allocation capacity, the dependency chain U ⇒ M ⇒ L ⇒ C cannot be grounded in U without vicious circularity. The mathematical core is an existence-and-profile theorem for a formal theory T whose axioms (intelligibility, well-founded dependence, undated mathematical necessity, semantic termination, and Gödel incompleteness) define a predicate Pure (x): we prove T ⊢ ∃!x Pure (x), with the unique instance D atemporal, non-spatial, necessary, simple, non-mechanical, and semantically self-present (𝒢(D, D), 𝒞(D) = D). Uniqueness is established order-theoretically—D is the least fixed point of a monotone grounding operator on a complete lattice of candidate grounds (Knaster–Tarski)—and non-mechanality is derived from incompleteness rather than stipulated, distinguishing the argument from Gödel’s own ontological proof, which stipulates its property profile and proves no uniqueness. As a physical congruence, we show that superluminal spacetime expansion is not generated by light-cone-bounded local processes, so the empirical world’s own global behaviour is not self-explanatory from within. Implications: The framework extends structural realism and Tegmark’s Mathematical Universe Hypothesis by establishing semantic grounding as co-fundamental with mathematical structure. The classical name for a unique, necessary, self-grounding ground of being and intelligibility is God; the result is confined to the derived profile and claims nothing beyond it. Consequences for ethics, philosophy of mind, and religion are left open.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Ockham ante una cuestión espinosa: ¿cómo conciliar la omnisciencia divina con la contingencia del futuro?
abstract: This paper deals with the controversy of the compatibility between divine omniscience and the contingency of future, concrete states of affairs. It attempts to make a formal reconstruction of William of Ockham’s solution in his Tractatus de praedestinatione et de praescientia Dei respectu futurorum contingentium. There is an alleged inconsistency between the following theses: (1) bivalence of future-tensed propositions (∀p ∈ Φ, ∀t ∈ T, ∀x ∈ ℕ: π (t, F(x) p) ∈ {0,1}); (2) necessity of the past (P(y)F(x)p ⊃ NP(y)F(x)p); and (3) divine infallibility (F(x)p ≡ DF(x)p). From these, a presumed modal collapse would follow: if at ta God knew that p would occur at tb (DF(x)p at ta), and if past truths are now necessary (NP(y)F(x)p), then it would follow that NF(x)p and therefore Np. Briefly, the precise assignment of a truth value would imply the necessity of the state of affairs denoted. Ockham, however, would show that this inference rests on false premises and there is no contradiction between maintaining God’s foreknowledge of the future, on the one hand, and the contingency of future concrete states of affairs, on the other. We will study his interpretation and formulation of the problem on the basis of his analysis of Chapter 9 of Aristotle’s Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας, and his formulation of the Aristotelian deterministic argument, which assumes a modal collapse between truth and necessity and implies that the Stagirite –according to Ockham’s reading– suspends the universal operativity of bivalence. Finally, we will show that the Ockhamist thesis represents an ordered and non-contradictory set of propositions and succeeds in generating a philosophically valid solution if interpreted within an appropriate formal framework of temporal logic. For the purposes of this analysis, the Ockhamist solution matches with a discrete instantaneous model of the type (T, <, dur, Φ, Ψ).

title: Navigating gods and monsters: the production of safe insecure spatialities in the deterrence of risk at sea
abstract: This study contributes the conceptualisation of ‘safe’ insecurity to existing literatures in critical Security Studies. To achieve this, this dissertation renders many concepts of International Relations that have developed to suit a terrestrial and solid understanding of the world as amphibious. This means that perils experienced at sea, particularly piracy, are represented to seafarers in tools that guide their transit of the 71% of the earth's surface that constitutes our oceans and seas subjectively and relatively – taking stock of the fluidity of the sea and human mobilities aboard merchant vessels as they propel the maritime spaces and places that are produced between ports. I explore literary and historical representations of maritime risk, such as Odysseus’ lengthy journey home from Troy and Sir Francis Drakes role as a spatial disruptor through the Colonial construct of the ‘privateer’. These discussions reveal that sea space has been represented and therefore lived differently based on its representation relative to the moment it is being experienced, which leads to specific rules of participation at sea that may be covert or overtly defined. These rules accentuate a binary of ‘God’ and ‘Monster’ relative to who is authenticated and excluded at sea. The empirical aspect of this dissertation applies this conceptual argument by drawing on the contemporary experience of navigating Somali piracy. It draws on the role of third-party maritime insurers (P&I Clubs) and seafarers to document how experiences of piracy have been used on land as the core knowledge that is mobilised to reproduce and refine practical deterrence measures that are used onboard merchant vessels. This analysis reveals that through exchanges of knowledge and expertise of life at sea, guidance is refined to embody the everyday norms of seafaring but, most importantly, pursues security without posing further risk to the merchant mariner. Drawing on personal testimonies of seafarers who have transited the aptly named High-Risk Area and the experience of elite, expert representatives of the maritime insurance industry, this study contributes the documentation of experiencing, representing and deterring piracy as part of a more extended, unfinished history of navigating risks at sea. Thesis embargoed until 31 December 2026.

title: RELIGIOUS BELIEFS AND CULTURE IN ANCIENT TIMES
abstract: This study analyzes the formation of early religious beliefs using a historical-developmental approach. It examines the emergence of religious concepts in human consciousness, their stages of development, and the characteristics of their origin in different regions from a scientific perspective. The research also explores the worldview of early human societies in adopting religious beliefs, as well as the influence of social and spiritual factors on this process. Furthermore, early forms of belief are considered in terms of their religious, scientific, historical, and modern interpretations, and their role and significance in the development of society are substantiated.

title: Apples and Oranges: Exaggerated Multiple Religious Belief in East Asia
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent scholarship proposes that East Asians commonly hold multiple religious beliefs simultaneously, even when they report a single religious identity or none at all. This note argues that this claim is substantially exaggerated due to a measurement mismatch: What Global East Survey (GES)‐based studies operationalize as religious belief is better understood as ambient cultural familiarity. Using probability sample data from the 2023 Pew Research Center Survey of Religion and Spirituality in East Asian Societies across Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, and Japan, I test whether the multiple religious belief pattern holds under more precise operationalization. When replicating the GES approach using cultural attachment items, the familiar pattern reproduces. When instead examining active devotion to specific deities, prevalence drops substantially, most sharply among Christians and religious nones, though the extent varies across societies. Comparing cultural attachment to religious belief is comparing apples to oranges.
venue: Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion

title: The Impact of Social Media Algorithms on Religious Belief Formation and Community Engagement
abstract: This study explores how social media algorithms influence the growth of religious beliefs and community involvement in today's digital landscape. As platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok increasingly suggest religious content through their algorithms, the way people make meaning of their faith is shaped not only by traditional religious institutions or personal decisions but also by data-driven personalization. Combining insights from social learning theory and mediated religion theory, the research takes an interdisciplinary approach, blending ideas from computer science and religious studies to examine both individual beliefs and collective religious interactions online. Data gathered from surveys of 400 active social media users and analysis of religious posts recommended by algorithms across major platforms reveal that these algorithms significantly affect exposure to religious ideas, reinforcing familiar themes and beliefs through repeated visibility. Many users reported that amplified algorithmic content influences their understanding of religious teachings and of what they consider credible beliefs. The findings also suggest that social media algorithms encourage religious community involvement by fostering virtual connections, promoting discussions, and strengthening a sense of belonging that complements offline religious practices. Additionally, the study notes a shift in religious authority, where metrics like likes, shares, and followers increasingly influence trust and credibility, sometimes more than traditional institutional or doctrinal authority. Despite being aware of algorithmic control, users still rely heavily on social media for religious learning, highlighting that awareness alone doesn’t fully mitigate algorithmic influence. Overall, the research indicates that while algorithms open new doors for religious engagement and community building, they also pose ethical and epistemological questions about authority, diversity, and the potential for beliefs to become more uniform. In summary, the study emphasizes the importance of digital religious literacy and ongoing interdisciplinary research to better understand how algorithms shape religious life in the digital age.

title: Choosing by religion: Similarity–attraction and religious beliefs in social media assessments
abstract: Abstract Social media assessments in selection increasingly expose applicants' religious beliefs, yet the implications of growing religious diversity in applicant pools remain underexplored. Leveraging social identity theory and the similarity–attraction paradigm, we examine how recruiters respond when applicants openly share their religious beliefs on social media (e.g., LinkedIn). To this end, U.S. working professionals evaluated an applicant's hireability based on a manipulated LinkedIn profile in a 4 (religious belief: Christian, Muslim, Jewish, control) by 2 (qualification: low vs. high) design. In Study 1 ( N = 372), a religion‐stratified sample screened a mid‐20s female applicant. In Study 2 ( N = 294), participants screened a mid‐60s male applicant. Across both studies, we found that similarity in religious beliefs increased raters' liking of the applicant, which in turn predicted ratings of task performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and overall hireability (e.g., interview invitations), above and beyond the applicant's actual qualifications. This bias was further shaped by both individual (rater religiosity, Study 1) and contextual moderators (news engagement with a religiously charged event, i.e., the Israel–Hamas War). Together, our findings position similarity perceptions as a central mechanism through which religious beliefs and social media assessments can influence hiring decisions.

title: Person-country Fit and Subjective Well-Being: The Roles of Religious Beliefs
abstract: While previous studies have extensively examined the relationship between religion and subjective well-being (SWB), findings remain mixed, and ongoing debates persist regarding the nature and strength of this association. Moreover, less is known about specific dimensions of religiosity, such as the importance of God in individuals’ lives and its relationship with SWB. Building on the person-country fit literature, this study analyzes the implications of (a) the fit between personal importance of God and country-level religiosity norms for SWB, and (b) the fit between personal importance of God and societal freedom of religion for SWB. Utilizing data from 78 countries and regions ( N = 114,441), the findings reveal that cultural fit—specifically, alignment between individual-level and country-level importance of God—is significantly associated with higher SWB, with this association being particularly strong among older adults. These results provide valuable empirical and theoretical insights, offering important implications for research on religion, person-country fit in religiosity, and SWB.
venue: Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology

title: South African Quakers about their religious beliefs and practices (2024–2025)
abstract: The following metadata consist of quotes or direct notes based on statements made by Quakers in South Africa. The data were collected through in-depth interviews, private conversations, and a focus group between December 2024 and May 2025. As the interviews contain the respondents' personal—and often intimate—stories, I have selected excerpts that focus on their religion. The data have been anonymized to protect the respondents' well-being.

title: Cultural and Religious Beliefs and Acceptance of Facial Cosmetic Surgery in Saudi Arabia
abstract: Background: This study examines the acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery in Saudi Arabia and the influence of social, cultural, and religious factors on public attitudes. It aims to improve the understanding of these factors to support patient education and informed decision-making. Methods: A cross‑sectional study was conducted using a validated, self‑administered electronic questionnaire distributed across all 13 regions of Saudi Arabia. Saudi adults aged 18 years or older who could read Arabic and consented to participate were included, whereas non‑Saudis, individuals younger than 18 years, and questionnaires with incomplete responses were excluded. A total of 1027 eligible participants completed the survey (with a completion rate of 55.7%). The questionnaire assessed demographics, history of facial cosmetic procedures, reasons for considering surgery, religious and cultural beliefs, and surgeon preferences. Associations were analyzed using χ 2 tests, with significance set at a P value of less than 0.05. Results: Acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery showed significant associations with sex, income, and occupation ( P < 0.001). Religious factors demonstrated strong relationships with acceptance, including perceived alignment with Islamic teachings and prior consultation with a religious scholar ( P < 0.001). Surgeon gender preference was also significantly associated with acceptance, whereas cultural influence alone did not show comparable statistical significance. Conclusions: Acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery in Saudi Arabia is shaped primarily by religious beliefs, medical necessity, and demographic factors. Religious permissibility plays a more influential role than cultural norms. These findings highlight the importance of culturally sensitive, religion‑aware counseling to support informed decision-making.
venue: Plastic & Reconstructive Surgery Global Open

title: Influence of Cultural and Religious Beliefs on Family Planning Decisions in Nigeria: A Narrative Review
abstract: Background: Nigeria continues to experience high fertility rates and low uptake of modern contraceptive methods despite decades of family planning (FP) programming. Cultural and religious beliefs remain central to reproductive decision-making and significantly shape attitudes toward fertility regulation. Aim and scope: This narrative review synthesizes empirical evidence on how cultural and religious beliefs influence family planning decisions in Nigeria, with attention to gender norms, regional variations, and health system interactions. Methods: A narrative review approach was employed. Peer-reviewed articles, demographic reports, and grey literature were retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online (AJOL). Studies published in English focusing on Nigeria were included. Thematic synthesis was used to organize findings. Key themes: Pronatalist norms, gender power asymmetries, son preference, misconceptions about contraception, religious doctrines, and the role of faith leaders emerged as dominant themes. These factors intersect with education, poverty, and health system accessibility to shape contraceptive behavior. Implications: Family planning programs in Nigeria must adopt culturally sensitive and faith informed strategies, strengthen male involvement, and address gender inequities. Future research should focus on longitudinal and intervention-based studies that integrate cultural and religious contexts.

title: Counter-Inductive Ideational Immunity and the Maintenance of Religious Belief: Introducing the CICI Project
abstract: Sincere, thoughtful, and etiologically similar people persist in mutually contrary religious commitments across generations, without converging and without obvious irrationality. In Problems of Religious Luck: Assessing the Limits of Reasonable Religious Disagreement (PRL, or Axtell 2020a) I argued that this stability is best understood through Counter-Inductive Ideational Immunity (CICI): a coordinated battery of cognitive and affective strategies that treat recognized disagreement and etiological symmetry not as reasons to reduce confidence or revise beliefs and attitudes but as pressure to be neutralized so that the commitment is preserved. This paper introduces the CICI Project — a program that carries forward that taxonomy of strategies and mechanisms from philosophical description into a measurable model. [Collaborators are sought to help carry through the study or a future iteration of it, collect, analyze and publish the data; contact author]
venue: PhilPapers (PhilPapers Foundation)

title: Faith in the Digital Age: Social Media's Impact on Religious Beliefs and Practices of Nigerian Youth
abstract: In contemporary Nigeria, the convergence of technological advancement and religious practices is becoming an increasingly important area of scholarly inquiry. this research investigates the influence that social media platforms have on the spiritual development and religious participation of young people in Nigeria. The purpose of this study is to examine both the opportunities and challenges that social media presents to established theological frameworks. This is achieved through a review of relevant studies and contemporary trends related to the topic. The findings indicate that social media has broadened the scope of religious content and made it possible to establish spiritual communities. On the other hand, it has also raised concerns over the validity of religious authority and the preservation of traditional practices in the face of new influences. This research contributes to the growing conversation about religion in Africa by providing insights into the shifting ways in which Nigerian young people exhibit their faith during this time period. in the contemporary digital environment.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Personal Identity Domains among Adolescents in Indonesia: Salience of Religious Beliefs and Purpose in Life
abstract: Research on adolescent identity has largely focused on developmental processes, while the content or domains of personal identity that are salient among adolescents within specific cultural contexts have not been systematically mapped. This gap is important because historically used domain lists may not be relevant for certain populations, including adolescents in Indonesia. This study aims to map the personal identity domains that are most frequently thought about (salience) and most clearly understood (clarity) among adolescents in Indonesia. Participants consisted of 454 adolescents aged 10-18 years (M = 14.49, SD = 2.51) in Indonesia. Data were collected using the Personal Identity Domain Questionnaire, which measures salience and clarity across 30 identity domains. The results indicated that religious beliefs and purpose in life emerged as the domains with the highest levels of salience and clarity among Indonesian adolescents. These findings suggest that certain identity domains are more prominent than others in terms of salience and clarity. Overall, these findings provide a descriptive empirical map of variation across personal identity domains, highlighting the contextual nature of identity content among adolescents in Indonesia.
venue: Islamic Guidance and Counseling Journal

title: The Effect of Religious Belief on Spiritual Tourism Intention: A Case Study of Vietnamese Tourists to Thailand
abstract: In this paper, religious belief was integrated into the Goal-Directed Behaviour Model, to clarify the behaviour of tourists towards spiritual tourism. Data from 516 Vietnamese tourists visiting Thailand was used for PLS-SEM analysis. The research results indicated positive relationships of religious belief to the original elements of the MGB, including attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control, emotion, and spiritual tourism intention. Desire was shown to be a key predictor of intention, mediating the effects of attitude, subjective norm, behavioural control, and emotion on the tourists’ intention to engage in spiritual tourism.
venue: Arrow - TU Dublin (Technological University Dublin)

title: Personal Data Revealing Religious Beliefs with a Focus on the Right to be Forgotten (GDPR Art. 17) in the Context of Poland
abstract: The problem addressed: The tension between the right to be forgotten (GDPR art. 17) and the autonomy of religious associations in processing personal data revealing religious beliefs, with particular reference to the Catholic Church in Poland. The aim of the research conducted: To examine the legal relationship between the right to privacy and the right to religious freedom under Polish and European law, and to assess the scope and limits of the right to be forgotten in the context of church data processing. Methods: Doctrinal-legal method of interpretation, supported by analysis of case law and supervisory practice. The results of the research: The article identifies the specifics of data processing regulations within the Catholic Church in Poland, clarifies the legal and supervisory practice context, and establishes the significance of the exception provided by Article 91 GDPR concerning the autonomy of religious associations in the realm of data protection. The conclusions drawn from the research: The right to be forgotten is not absolute; its application in the religious context must take into account constitutional frameworks, the specificity of canon law, and the need to balance individual rights with the institutional rights of religious communities.
venue: Prawo Kanoniczne

title: The Luo Indigenous Religious Beliefs and Cultural Practices of Environmental Preservation: A Case of Lower Nyakach: Kisumu County, Kenya
abstract: Environmental degradation remains one of the greatest challenges confronting humanity despite advances in science, technology, and environmental policy. In many African societies, indigenous religious beliefs and cultural practices have historically played a significant role in regulating human interaction with nature. However, modernization, Christianity, formal education, globalization, and socio-economic transformations have altered traditional environmental management systems. This study examined the persistence of indigenous religious beliefs and cultural practices that promote environmental preservation among the Luo community of Lower Nyakach in Kisumu County, Kenya. Specifically, it investigated the extent to which traditional ecological knowledge continues to influence environmental stewardship despite increasing exposure to foreign religions and modern lifestyles. The study employed a mixed-methods research design, integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data were collected through questionnaires, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and observation. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Bayesian correlation analysis, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. Findings revealed that although indigenous environmental beliefs have declined due to modernization and religious transformation, many traditional conservation practices continue to shape community attitudes toward biodiversity conservation, sacred sites, vegetation protection, and sustainable farming. Sacred forests, protection of particular plant and animal species, respect for ancestral sites, and the continued use of indigenous agricultural practices remain important mechanisms of environmental stewardship. Nevertheless, harmful beliefs, declining traditional authority and reduced intergenerational transmission of indigenous knowledge threaten the sustainability of these practices. The study concludes that indigenous religious beliefs remain an essential component of community-based environmental conservation and recommends integrating indigenous ecological knowledge into national environmental policies, educational curricula, and community conservation programmes to strengthen sustainable environmental management.
venue: International Journal of Environmental Protection and Policy

title: Spiritual and Religious Beliefs, Behaviors, and Struggles in Relation to Death Anxiety: Evidence from a U.S. Nationwide Probability Sample
abstract: Death anxiety is associated with adverse psychological and health outcomes, yet findings regarding the role of religiosity and spirituality (R/S) as protective or risk factors remain mixed. Prior research has relied on convenience samples, combined disparate R/S constructs, and rarely tested nonlinear associations. This study examined associations between death anxiety and multiple R/S facets in a nationwide probability sample of 3,010 U.S. adults. Regression models tested associations between R/S predictors and death anxiety and tested moderation by age and chronic illness, controlling for demographics, meaning in life, social support, anxiety, and depression. All belief predictors (afterlife beliefs, R/S centrality, R/S peace, and positive view of God) showed curvilinear inverted U-shaped patterns: strong worldviews, both religious and secular, were linked to lower death anxiety, while ambivalence was associated with the highest death anxiety. Regarding behaviors, Bible reading was linearly protective; however, church attendance and prayer were protective only at threshold levels (multiple times per month and week, respectively). R/S struggles (insecure attachment to God and negative view of God) were consistently detrimental. Age moderated several relationships, with R/S centrality, peace, positive view of God, and prayer becoming increasingly protective in later life, while avoidant attachment to God became more harmful. Chronic illness moderated only positive God views such that benevolent God beliefs became more protective with increasing illness burden. These findings clarify inconsistencies in the existing literature and suggest that clarity in one's worldview may be an important target for intervention.
venue: Journal of Religion and Health

title: Religious beliefs and practices, political orientation, and distrust in healthcare predict attitudes toward mRNA vaccines in the United States
abstract: Religion has contributed to societal divides regarding COVID-19 mRNA vaccines. In this study, we conducted a secondary analysis of a survey of U.S. adults (N = 4939) focused on how religious affiliations, beliefs, and practices impact attitudes toward genetic and genomic activities, one of which was mRNA vaccines. The dataset included large samples of participants from six religious groups in the U.S. (Black Protestant, Catholic, Evangelical Protestant, Jewish, Mainline Protestant, and Muslim), as well as individuals who were atheist, agnostic, or spiritual. ANCOVA results indicated that Evangelical Protestant participants showed significantly less support for mRNA vaccines than other groups, while atheist participants were the most supportive. Muslim participants had the highest concerns, whereas atheist participants had the lowest. Regression analyses indicated the strongest predictors of support for mRNA vaccines were more spiritual community support for community health, followed by higher acceptance of evolution, more liberal political orientation, less distrust toward the healthcare system, higher frequency of attending religious activities, higher income, lower fundamentalist religious beliefs, and more spiritual community support for liberal reproductive and end of life views. The strongest predictors of concerns about mRNA vaccines were more distrust toward the healthcare system and more conservative political orientation, followed by less spiritual community support for community health, stronger beliefs about God in the body, more fundamentalist religious beliefs, and lower knowledge of genetics. The large sample size and examination of a broad array of religious variables alongside distrust and political orientation offer new insights. These findings add to the literature on the culture wars surrounding mRNA vaccines, and can perhaps aid in future efforts to build trust and relationships between public health and religious communities.
venue: PLOS Global Public Health

title: A Reflection on the Relationship Between Literature and Religious Beliefs: A Case Study of Persian Textbooks for the Second Cycle of Secondary Education
abstract: The present study aimed to explain and analyze the intertextual relationships between the fundamental components of religion and literature in Persian-language textbooks used in the second cycle of secondary education. This article is based on the premise that religious and literary texts should not be regarded as two entirely separate domains; rather, because of their shared linguistic, symbolic, and meaning-making functions, they have consistently interacted with and influenced one another. Accordingly, the relationship between religion and literature in Persian textbooks for the second cycle of secondary education was analyzed with particular emphasis on doctrinal components. The study employed a descriptive-analytical research method, based on the assumption that every literary work is, in some way, connected to and indebted to sacred and religious texts. The data-collection instrument was developed according to standardized content-analysis components. Following a review of the theoretical foundations, the instrument was organized around three principal categories: the principles of religion, the subsidiary duties of religion, and ethics. Based on the importance coefficient index, attention to religious components and their relationship with literature was found to be uneven. In Grade 10, the greatest emphasis was placed on the principles of religion, while the subsidiary duties of religion received the least attention. In Grades 11 and 12, the principles of religion similarly received the greatest attention, whereas ethics received the least. Within the category of the principles of religion, monotheism received the greatest emphasis in Grades 10 and 12, while prophethood was mentioned most frequently in Grade 11. In the Grade 10 Persian textbook, the greatest emphasis was placed on enjoining what is right; in Grade 11, on jihad; and in Grade 12, on forbidding what is wrong. Within the ethical category, the greatest emphasis was placed on honesty in Grade 10, integrity in Grade 11, and courage in Grade 12.
venue: Treasury of Persian Language and Literature

title: ‘God didn’t like it and detained them not to fly again:’ evolutionary understanding, acceptance, and perceived conflicts of students with interwoven religious beliefs
abstract: Evolution is challenging to teach because many students hold non-scientific conceptions and reject evolution due to perceived conflicts with their religion, values, cultures, or beliefs. Extensive research has been carried out in the Global North on students’ evolutionary understanding, acceptance, and conflict perceptions. This research has led to considerably different findings depending on the sample’s socio-cultural environment. In the Global South, less research has been conducted, and findings may be divergent from the Global North, especially in populations where both a monotheistic, Abrahamic world-religion and an indigenous religion are relevant, as is the case in Namibia. Thus, we conducted a questionnaire study with N = 221 upper-secondary Namibian students. The students struggled to understand evolution, having few scientific conceptions and more non-scientific conceptions, with some of them being culture-specific. They reported moderate evolutionary acceptance and perceived conflicts. Higher religious faith correlated with higher perceptions of conflicts. Evolutionary understanding was positively related to evolutionary acceptance. The findings indicate that enhancing evolutionary understanding and reducing perceived conflicts of religious students through inclusive and culturally-sensitive strategies may support students in accepting and learning about evolution. We especially propose implications for students with interwoven religious beliefs.

title: The Application of the Integrative Biology-Fiqh Approach to Improving Scientific Literacy and Religious Beliefs of Students at Muhammadiyah Senior High School in Bima City
abstract: The dichotomy between religious knowledge and science in the madrasah education system in Indonesia has created an epistemological gap that hinders the development of students' scientific literacy and erodes the depth of their religious beliefs. This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of the Biology-Fiqh integrative approach in improving scientific literacy and religious beliefs of students at Madrasah Aliyah Muhammadiyah in Bima City. This study adopted a quasi-experimental design with a pre-test-post-test control group design involving 68 eleventh-grade students divided into an experimental group (n=34) and a control group (n=34). The research instruments included an adapted PISA 2022 framework-based scientific literacy test, a validated religious belief scale, a cognitive engagement observation sheet, and a semi-structured interview guide. Data analysis used ANCOVA, Cohen's d effect size test, and thematic analysis for qualitative data. The results showed that the experimental group experienced a significant increase in scientific literacy (M gain = 28.4; d = 1.12; p < 0.001) compared to the control group (M gain = 11.7; d = 0.48). Religious belief also increased significantly in the experimental group (M gain = 19.6; d = 0.89; p < 0.001). Qualitative analysis revealed four main themes: transformation of epistemological perspectives, strengthening of Muslim-scientist identity, resolution of cognitive conflict between science and religion, and learning motivation based on religious meaning-making. This study contributes to the development of a contextual integrative pedagogical model for madrasahs in eastern Indonesia and offers an operational framework for teachers in implementing science integration based on Islamic values.
venue: Attractive Innovative Education Journal

title: Mekanisme Kognitif Niat Beli Produk Kosmetik Halal: Peran Mediasi Halal Awareness pada Pengaruh Religious Belief dan Sertifikasi Halal
abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of religious belief and halal certification on purchase intention of Safi halal cosmetic products, with halal awareness as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed using a survey method involving 170 potential consumers in Malang City who were aware of Safi products but had never made a purchase. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Square–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 3 software. The results indicate that religious belief and halal certification have a positive and significant effect on halal awareness and purchase intention. Furthermore, halal awareness is proven to have a positive and significant influence on purchase intention and partially mediates the relationship between religious belief and halal certification on purchase intention. These findings suggest that stronger religious values and clear halal certification enhance consumers’ halal awareness, which subsequently increases their intention to purchase halal cosmetic products.
venue: JEMSI (Jurnal Ekonomi Manajemen dan Akuntansi)

title: Sacred landscapes of Turan: religious beliefs, ritual practices and mythological traditions of ancient Central Asia in written sources (based on Khwandamir's "Maosir al-Muluk") and some archaeological sources
abstract: This thesis examines the religious beliefs, ritual practices, and mythological traditions attributed to the peoples of ancient Turan - the historical-geographical macro-region of Central Asia comprising Bactria, Sogdiana, Khwarazm, Margiana, and Fergana. Drawing on Avestan literature, Greek and Latin ethnographic accounts (Herodotus, Strabonn, Arrian, Quintus Curtius Rufus), and archaeological evidence from Bronze Age through Late Antique sites, the study reconstructs the layered religious landscape of the region: pre-Zoroastrian nature cults, the gradual and uneven spread of Zoroastrian doctrine, and epic-mythological figures such as Tur/Afrasiyab and Siyavush. The thesis argues, following recent source-critical scholarship, that "Turan" was never a single ethnic or confessional community but a shifting literary, geographical, and religious construct whose content changed considerably between the Avestan age, the classical period, and the medieval Perso-Islamic epic tradition. Methodological problems of extrapolating from later legendary sources onto earlier historical periods are given particular attention. title: Religious Persecution in Communist Albania through Constitutional and Legal Acts
abstract: Following the victory of the communist regime in 1944, the new Albanian state built its institutions on a materialist worldview that stood in direct opposition to the universal principles of freedom of conscience and religious belief. The state progressively restricted religious practice until it banned it altogether. This anti-religious campaign proceeded along two tracks: anti-religious political propaganda and the adoption of legal acts prohibiting the practice of religion. A 1967 decree-law banned religious belief outright, and the 1976 Constitution declared Albania the first atheist state in the world. This paper is based on an analysis of legal acts, scholarly literature, archival documents, and contemporary testimony. Through these measures the regime banned religious belief and confiscated the property of religious communities, while subjecting clergy to harsh punitive measures: internment, imprisonment, torture, and execution. The study rests on comparative, historical, and normative methods. The ban on religion sought to replace God with the figures of communism, in the service of a world communist revolution. The results show that religious belief was not an obstacle to the development of communist society; the principal obstacle was the state-controlled economy.
venue: Occasional Papers on Religion in Eastern Europe

title: Exploring the link between Religion and Subjective Well-Being in Europe. Are Education and Innovation the Third Wheel?
abstract: This paper empirically explores the relationship between religious beliefs, happiness and life satisfaction in Europe, considering the role of education. We use the European Values Study 2017, which includes Northern, Southern, Western and Eastern European countries and countries at the boundary of West Asia and Eastern Europe. The analysis is extended to innovation contexts. An instrumental variable approach is employed to address endogeneity in religious variables. The findings reveal that the importance of God is positively correlated to life satisfaction and negatively to happiness but the sign shifts to positive when religious beliefs are endogenous. Religious attendance is positively linked to happiness and life satisfaction. Education appears to have no bearing on how religiosity and SWB are related.
venue: Socio-Economic Planning Sciences

title: Socio-economic status and health seeking behaviour of civil servants in Odukpani Local Government Area of Cross River State, Nigeria
abstract: The main thrust of the paper is to examine socio-economic status and health seeking behaviour of civil servants in Odukpani Local Government Area of Cross River State. Health-seeking Behaviors (HSB) are closely linked with the health status of a nation, and thus its economic development. The paper explores the interplay between access to health insurance and religious belief as it relates to health seeking behaviour of civil servants. The Health Belief Model (HBM) was used as the theoretical framework in the study. The cross-sectional survey was adopted as the research design. The sample size for the study consists of one hundred (100) respondents working in Odukpani council secretariat and the samples were taken through Cochran's sample determination size. Likert Scale Questionnaire was used as an instrument of data collection and the data were analyzed using Pearson product moment correlation analysis. The hypotheses were tested at 0.05 level of significance. The finding revealed that access to health insurance and religious belief positively affect health seeking behaviour. Based on the findings, it was recommended that comprehensive health insurance policies should be available and accessible to all civil servants, covering contractual and temporary employees. Religious leaders and organizations should promote health education and services that align with religious beliefs of civil servants.
venue: Afrischolar Discovery

title: Social learning of scientific and religious views: parents as transmission agents and their approaches against dissent
abstract: Focusing on two prominent belief frameworks – science and religion – this study examined adults’ retrospective perceptions of the role their parents played in transmitting and maintaining beliefs. We adapted a previous method (McLoughlin, 2021) and asked Australian and Malaysian adults to reflect on whether and how their current scientific and religious beliefs were influenced by their parents. Across both countries, adults indicated that their parents were influential for both science and religion. Participants generally recalled scientific influence positively irrespective of how religious they were. For religion, greater participant religiosity was associated with positive influence for Australian adults only. Approximately three-quarters of Malaysian participants identified their parents as the only source for both religious and scientific beliefs. While the same proportion of Australians indicated so for science, significantly less Australian participants identified their parents as the only source for religious beliefs. When reflecting on how their parents approached conflicting views between themselves and their parents, Australian participants generally reported that their parents employed a supportive approach across both domains. Malaysian participants often reported that their parents, though open to accepting dissenting scientific beliefs with a supportive stance, were more inclined toward a directive approach when faced with conflicts in religious views. This study affords novel insights into the universality and variation of parents’ roles in the transmission and maintenance of scientific and religious beliefs across diverse populations.
venue: Open Access Victoria University of Wellington | Te Herenga Waka (Figshare)

title: RELIGIOSITY AND MEDITATION PRACTICE: EXPLORING THEIR EXPLANATORY POWER ON PSYCHOLOGICAL ADJUSTMENT
abstract: Religiosity is a multidimensional construct that incorporates different domains, including ideological and devotional aspects such as religious beliefs and prayer, which might have an impact on psychological adjustment. Psychological adjustment could also be improved through the systematic cultivation of the contemplative practices of meditation, such as focused attention (FA), open monitoring (OM) and compassion meditation (CM), which could differentially affect psychological adjustment depending on the conditions of practice. The aim of this study was to assess the explanatory power of religious beliefs and the practice of prayer, FA, OM and CM on psychological adjustment, considering some practice-related variables such as total practice experience, session length, frequency of practice, and lifetime practice. Psychological adjustment was assessed by means of happiness, positive affect, depression, negative affect and emotional overproduction. A cross-sectional design was used, with a final sample comprising 210 Spanish participants who completed an online assessment protocol. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed, including age and sex in the first step, with the addition of religious beliefs and the practice of prayer, FA, OM and CM in the second step. The total practice experience of FA significantly contributed to improvement in happiness (β = 0.21; p = 0.023), and to the reduction of negative affect (β = -0.23; p = 0.012). FA session length was significantly related to all the psychological adjustment outcomes: happiness (β = 0.25; p = 0.001), positive affect (β = 0.17; p = 0.016), depression (β = -0.27; p < 0.001), negative affect (β = -0.26; p < 0.001) and emotional overproduction (β = -0.22; p = 0.002). CM practice frequency was significantly associated with happiness (β = 0.16; p = 0.048). Lifetime practice of OM was significantly related to decrements in emotional overproduction (β = -0.21; p = 0.028). Religious beliefs and prayer seemed to be less relevant than meditation practices such as FA, OM and CM in explaining psychological adjustment. The distinct meditation practices might be differentially related to distinct psychological adjustment outcomes, through different practice-related variables. However, research into other forms of institutional religiosity integrating social aspects of religion seems mandatory.
venue: ICPSR Data Holdings

title: Traces from the Ancient in the Faith of Anatolian People
abstract: Anatolian geography has hosted numerous civilizations as from the earliest times of the history for its geopolitical position. The religious beliefs had been effective on the living styles of the communities in every period of the history. People reflected the practices related with their beliefs on their daily life. Many cultural practices performed in our present day show great similarities with the religious beliefs and rituals of Ancient Anatolia. In this study, it was attempted to identify the folk belief and customs which had existed in the ancient times of Anatolia and have reached up to our present day. Today, we have knowledge related with the subject matter on Kültepe tablets that are the first documents of Anatolia written in cuneiform script and documents belonging to the people living in Anatolia in the upcoming dates. Particularly, Kültepe records and Hittite documents belonging to the Era of Assyrian Trade Colonies provide illuminative information. In the study, the afore-said documents were analyzed and the similarities with the customs of the present day were presented. Numerous beliefs and traditions such as incubus and evil-eye belief, rain prayer, holiness attribution on natural assets and animals, lamenting tradition have reached up to our present day from the ancient times of the history by getting richer. When we look at the information obtained from the cuneiform documents we have examined and the practices applied in today's Anatolia, it is understood that religious beliefs and rituals, which had an important place in the lives of ancient societies, are still maintained in today's Anatolian folk beliefs and traditions, with some changes.
venue: International Journal of Ancient History

title: Религиозные представления местного населения Средней Азии в эпоху эллинизма
abstract: В статье рассматриваются религиозные верования населения Средней Азии в эллинистическую эпоху (IV–II вв. до н. э.) на основе археологических, нумизматических и эпиграфических источников. Анализируется роль Ахура-Мазды, Митры, Вахш–Окса и Анахиты в религиозных представлениях местного населения. Отдельное внимание уделяется сохранению традиционных культов переселённого греко-македонского населения. Рассматривается сосуществование местных и греческих религиозных традиций, а также проблема их возможного взаимовлияния и синкретизма. Religious beliefs of the local population of Central Asia in the Hellenistic period The article examines the religious beliefs of the population of Central Asia during the Hellenistic period (4th–2nd centuries BCE) based on archaeological, numismatic, and epigraphic evidence. It analyzes the role of Ahura Mazda, Mithra, Vakhsh-Oxus, and Anakhita in the religious beliefs of local communities. Particular attention is given to the continuation of traditional cults among the Greek-Macedonian population settled in Central Asia. The coexistence, interaction, and possible syncretism of local and Greek religious traditions are also considered. Mahalliy va yunon diniy an'analarining birgalikda mavjudligi hamda ehtimoliy o'zaro ta'siriga e'tibor qaratiladi.

title: REPRESENTATION OF THE NATIONAL AND RELIGIOUS VALUES OF THE UZBEK PEOPLE IN NINETEENTH- AND TWENTIETH-CENTURY SOURCES
abstract: This article analyzes the representation of the national and religious values of the Uzbek people in the sources of the 19th–20th centuries. Based on written materials of this period, the study examines the customs, traditions, religious beliefs, and spiritual values of the people. In addition, ethnocultural information reflected in these sources reveals the features of social life and cultural development of Uzbek society.
